Ornella Tchuente, founder of the Indice Influence Africaine(TM): "Talon embodies the silent authority that builds a lasting legacy"

La Nation Benin...

Ornella Tchuente, an image and influence strategist, founder of the Influence Africaine(TM) framework, recently distinguished herself with an assessment, through several prisms, of the Beninese head of state, whose singular leadership is, according to her, made of silent authority and generational vision. Through the present interview, she decodes the foundations of that framework.

La Nation: What motivated the initiative of the Indice d'Influence Africaine(TM) (African Influence Index)?

Ornella Tchuente: My vision is clear: to build an elite of ethical and strategic influencers who, through their stance, their choices and their legacy, transform the perception and the place of Africa in the world. I refuse to have our African models read through outside prisms that minimise or distort their influence. I therefore created the Indice d'Influence Africaine(TM), an unprecedented methodology that makes it possible to measure influence in a rooted way.

On the basis of this barometer, you describe Patrice Talon as the "archetype of the president-entrepreneur". What, in his career, in your view, makes him a unique model in Africa?

Patrice Talon perfectly illustrates this figure of the president-entrepreneur, because he first built his legitimacy through the economy before translating it into the exercise of political power. His path is singular: starting from a highly strategic sector, cotton, he built an empire that earned him the nickname "King of Cotton". This economic success was not an end in itself, but a springboard towards a broader influence, where management experience, rigour and entrepreneurial logic became political assets.

What distinguishes him is his capacity to apply the reflexes of the entrepreneur to governance: a long-term vision rather than the management of the everyday, efficiency and discipline rather than political agitation. His style of governance can be described as a "dictatorship of efficiency": few populist speeches, a great deal of rigour in the follow-up of projects. He is therefore not the archetype of the traditional politician, but that of an architect of development, capable of articulating economic ambition, a vision of governance and operational efficiency.

Patrice Talon embodies a generation of African leaders who demonstrate that one can move from the world of business to the public sphere without renouncing one's codes, but by placing them at the service of the collective. It is in this that he represents a benchmark for Africa: the demonstration that a leader can combine private economic success and lasting public impact.

Your Indice d'Influence Africaine(TM) is very different from the classic popularity rankings. In what way does your grid renew the way of analysing leadership?

The Indice d'Influence Africaine(TM) distinguishes itself from traditional rankings because it does not stop at visibility or digital popularity. Too often, leadership is confused with media presence, number of followers or ephemeral buzz. Yet these criteria are incapable of reflecting the depth and singularity of African influence. The grid proposes a paradigm shift: it measures the essence of influence, not its facade. It rests on five cultural and strategic dimensions that reveal the true reach of a leader: silent authority, influencing without noise, being quoted even in one's absence; deliberate legacy, embodying a rooted and transmissible identity; selective radiance, choosing one's spaces of impact rather than being everywhere; temporal transcendence, building a legacy that outlasts news cycles; symbolic density, creating an immediately recognisable signature.

In other words, the Index does not ask: "Who makes the most noise?" It answers rather the question: "Who will leave a lasting, coherent and respected trace?" It is a more qualitative, rooted and strategic approach that profoundly renews the way of analysing African leadership, giving it back its own codes rather than evaluating it through external standards.

Benin is posting sustained growth. But the World Bank points to the challenges of productivity and inclusion. How do you reconcile economic growth and the quality of growth in your assessment?

Economic growth, when it is expressed solely in figures, can give a flattering but incomplete image. A country can post +6% of GDP, but if this dynamic does not translate into inclusion, productivity and equitable redistribution, its impact remains limited in the real life of citizens.

In my approach with the Indice d'Influence Africaine(TM), I consider that the value of a leadership is measured not only by raw economic performance, but by the quality of the transformation produced. This connects with two essential dimensions of my grid: temporal transcendence, do the reforms and investments create durable foundations that will survive political cycles? Deliberate legacy: are the choices of governance rooted in a cultural and societal vision that elevates the people as a whole?

In the case of Benin, growth is undeniable, but the challenge is now to transform this performance into inclusive growth: strengthening education and access to opportunities for young people, improving agricultural and industrial productivity so as not to depend solely on services or cotton, ensuring that women, rural communities and the middle classes benefit directly from this dynamic.

You award 10/10 in "temporal transcendence" thanks to Vision 2060 Alafia. What proves, in your view, that this project goes beyond a mere announcement effect?

I would say that an announcement captivates the moment, but a vision captivates generations.

Most African political projects suffer from a recurrent ill. They shine at the moment of their launch, but disappear into oblivion for lack of continuity or credibility. Vision 2060 Alafia, on the contrary, carries within it several elements that reflect a real will to go beyond the announcement effect. First, symbolic coherence. The very choice of the word "Alafia", which means peace and prosperity in Yoruba, anchors the vision in a culture and a collective memory. We are not dealing with an imported slogan, but with a project that speaks the language of its people. This cultural dimension is essential to longevity: a project rooted in an identity resists time better.

Next, the institutional architecture: Vision 2060 Alafia is not limited to a presidential promise; it is structured around programmes, infrastructure and measurable monitoring frameworks. One sees this through the establishment of industrial zones, cultural diplomacy and investments in strategic infrastructure that exceed the electoral calendar.

Finally, the effect of generational projection: to think 2060 is already to inscribe Benin beyond a mandate, beyond a political cycle. It is to accept that the fruits will not be harvested by a single leader but by a succession of generations. This temporal humility, rare in politics, is in itself a sign of transcendence.

Obviously, like any vision, Alafia will be judged on its capacity to keep its promises over time. But today it has already crossed an important threshold: it has created a collective hope. And a vision that becomes shared hope ceases to be a mere announcement effect and begins to inscribe itself in history.

The Glo-Djigbe Industrial Zone (Gdiz) is presented as a turning point. What criteria do you use to measure its true impact beyond the announced figures?

My role, through the Indice d'Influence Africaine(TM), is not to compete with economists, but to observe how a project inscribes itself in a trajectory of leadership and legacy. For the Gdiz, the official figures speak for themselves: more than 10,000 direct jobs created according to the authorities, an integrated textile factory of world dimension being finalised, and already concrete exports, such as Made in Benin garments sent to U.S. Polo Assn. or 80,000 pieces delivered to Kiabi. These elements are public and verifiable. But beyond the statistics, my analytical grid rests on other criteria: the quality of the jobs, are they really bearers of a future for young people and women? The durability of the ecosystem: is the zone becoming a structuring framework, with its services, its certifications and a long-term vision? Citizen perception: do Beninese families concretely feel that their daily life is changing?

As an influence analyst, I therefore look at two things: the symbolic effect, is the Gdiz becoming a marker of national pride and continental radiance? The lived effect: do populations recognise themselves in this project, or do they perceive it as a distant showcase? It is this double gaze that makes it possible to evaluate whether the Gdiz is truly a turning point for Benin.

The Port of Cotonou has become a regional hub. In what way does this infrastructure strengthen President Talon's influence at the African level?

When I analyse President Patrice Talon's leadership through the Indice d'Influence Africaine(TM), I look not only at his speeches, but also at the concrete symbols that translate his vision. The Port of Cotonou is a striking example. It is today the economic lung of Benin, responsible for nearly 90% of external trade and contributing more than half of national GDP. And it is not just a statistic: in February 2025, the African Development Bank validated financing of 80 million euros to modernise and extend the port. This clearly shows that this infrastructure is perceived as strategic at the regional and international scale. Beyond the figures, what interests me are the symbolic effects. The Port of Cotonou has become an indispensable regional platform, notably for landlocked countries such as Niger, Burkina Faso or Mali. It is also an example of selective radiance: Benin did not seek to be everywhere, but invested in a precise hub that changes its weight in the sub-region. Finally, there is a dimension of temporal transcendence: the investments and international partnerships around this port go far beyond a presidential mandate. They form part of a generational logic. Let us not forget cultural soft power: the Port of Cotonou is not limited to its logistical performance. Its perimeter wall has become a veritable open-air work of art: a monumental fresco of 660 metres, already considered the longest in the world, with the ambition of extending progressively across all the port's walls to reach 1.3 km. This project, carried by a collective of graffiti artists, retraces the history of Benin and stages the coexistence between religions and communities. By transforming an economic infrastructure into a cultural symbol, Benin projects an image of openness, pride and creativity that goes beyond borders.

You speak of "selective radiance" on Facebook and Twitter/X. What counts most: the number of followers or the quality of the audience reached?

For me, the question of radiance is not reduced to a contest of figures. One can have a million followers and very little real impact, or have a more restricted audience but composed of key actors who relay, who quote and who really transform an image into influence.

In the Indice d'Influence Africaine(TM), selective radiance therefore does not measure mass, but relevance. What counts is: the quality of interactions, the capacity to dominate certain targeted spaces and above all the coherence between the message and the audience. In the case of President Patrice Talon, I do not have access to the precise statistics of his social networks. But even without these data, what one can observe is that he does not seek to be omnipresent or to saturate the digital space. He chooses his moments of speech, his channels and his timing, and it is precisely that which creates an effect of rarity and weight.

You assert that the "Beninese model" already inspires Lagos or Kigali. What is really transferable from this experience to other African countries?

I am above all an observer and strategist, not a master of universal solutions. My Indice d'Influence Africaine(TM) is built to bring to light the dynamics of durable, rooted and symbolic leadership. And when I speak of inspiration by the "Beninese model", it is precisely what I see working not as a scheme to be copied identically, but as a prism of reflection applicable elsewhere. Here are three quite concrete aspects, inspired by Benin, that I judge transferable, and which are already being noticed in contexts such as Kigali or Lagos: a generational vision, beyond the political cycle. Benin, with projects such as Vision 2060 Alafia or the extension of the port, shows how a state can think outside electoral mandates. I have observed this same stance in Kigali, which is already planning beyond 2040, and in Lagos, which is structuring its metropolitan development over the coming decades. The case of integrated infrastructure in the service of sub-regional influence, such as the Port of Cotonou. This positioning resonates in cities such as Lagos, which seek to become regional hubs. Finally, a symbolic and coherent leadership. The action of the port, of the industrial zones or of cultural diplomacy is perceived as embodied, coherent, rooted. It is this combination of efficiency and local storytelling that generates adhesion, and it is what cities such as Kigali are trying to reflect in their international stance.

Patrice Talon has announced that he would not seek a third term. How do you measure, in your Index, the resilience of a political system faced with the departure of such a leader?

The resilience of a political system is measured not only in its immediate stability, but in its capacity to continue functioning when a leader withdraws. The case of Patrice Talon is a strong illustration: his categorical refusal of a third term, confirmed on several occasions in 2025, inscribes his influence in an institutional dynamic rather than in a logic of personal power. In other words, resilience is built when institutions continue to embody a vision, even after the leader's departure. And it is precisely this continuity that makes the difference between a personal power and a truly architectural influence.

Finally, if you had to sum up Patrice Talon's influence in one formula, what would it be?

For me, Patrice Talon embodies the silent authority that builds a lasting legacy. He did not seek to seduce through noise, but to transform through structure, leaving a trace that goes beyond his mandate and is already inscribed in the history of Benin and of Africa.

a3453.t:
By MUBITA KATETE
THE Centre for Infectious Disease Research in Zambia (CIDRZ) has donated 10 oxygen concentrators to the University Teaching Hospital (UTH) – Children’s Hospital as part of its ongoing support for healthcare services in the country.
 Dr Mutumwa Muyangana, the Medical Officer for the USAID TB LON project said the 10 oxygen concentrators would improve patient care at the UTH-Children’s Hospital.
 “The USAID TB LON project, implemented by CIDRZ, has been working closely with both the Children’s Hospital and the Adult Hospital. I am delighted to hand over these oxygen concentrators as part of our ongoing support to the hospital,” Dr. Muyangana said
 She said the donation shows the strong partnership between CIDRZ, the Ministry of Health, and UTH’s management and staff.
 “This collaboration ensures that the patients, both children and adults, receive the best possible care,” Dr Muyangana said.
 She said the TB LON Project had been instrumental in supporting tuberculosis (TB) patients in tertiary hospitals across eight provinces.
 Dr. Muyangana explained that many patients who sought treatment at such hospitals presented more complex forms of TB, which often required respiratory support.
 “In some cases, patients require respiratory support even after completing TB treatment, due to complications arising from the disease itself. This highlights the need for advanced approaches in patient management, including the use of oxygen therapy,” she said.
 Dr. Muyangana was confident that the donated oxygen concentrators would provide essential support for patients with post-TB care needs, especially those who experienced respiratory complications from extensive lung damage caused by the disease.
 “We are confident that these concentrators will be put to good use, ensuring that patients in need of oxygen therapy can receive it promptly and effectively,” she said.
 “We are honoured to be able to contribute to this effort and look forward to continuing our support to strengthen healthcare in Zambia,” said Dr. Muyangana.

The relief and the emergency activities managed by Tigray Interim Administration is going well despite the rampant baseless disinformation, CEO Mulu Nega said.
Mulu said his administration is progressing well to achieve all the priorities set in the short and long term plans of the region.
He stressed that there is very huge demand in humanitarian assistance. But “the relief and the emergency activities are going well in the region.”
The CEO stated that the administration “has already started providing food for the needy population at all levels, and we have agreed with the responsible federal government sectors to speed up and strengthen the activities because people should get food and all basic necessities.”
The only thing that needs to be strengthened is the distribution to all woredas and cities as the flow is very good, he said, adding that this is also going well but will be strengthened to address all the population in the region.

a3534.t:
JOHANNESBURG – The fourth Intra-African Trade Fair (IATF2025) opened in Algiers, Algeria this week, with calls for greater economic integration and a renewed commitment to the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) – this is particularly relevant to the auto industry, with the Africa Automotive Show due to get underway tomorrow.
Addressing the opening ceremony, the Chairman of the IATF2025 Advisory Council and former Nigerian President, Chief Olusegun Obasanjo, described the fair as a symbol of Africa’s economic awakening. He noted that the event has become a major platform for connecting buyers, sellers, investors and governments from across the continent.
Obasanjo reported that 48 African countries are participating in exhibitions, marking the largest country participation since the inaugural fair in 2018. He highlighted the fair’s record of facilitating major deals, stating that the previous three editions had generated combined trade and investment commitments exceeding R2.2-trillion. He pointed to the Julius Nyerere Hydropower Project in Tanzania, a R54-billion deal signed at the 2018 fair, as an example of the transformational deals the event enables. In her address, African Union Commission Deputy Chairperson, Ambassador Selma Malika Haddadi, echoed this sentiment, noting that each edition of the fair has brought the continent closer to the goals of the African Union’s Agenda 2063. The Algiers fair is convened under the theme ‘Boosting Intra-African Trade for a Sustainable Future: Innovation, Value Addition and Green Industrialisation.’
Ambassador Haddadi stated that boosting intra-African trade is both an economic and political imperative. While Africa contributes only 2.9 per cent to global trade, intra-African trade has been growing, expanding by 27 per cent between 2017 and 2023 to approach R3.7 trillion.
She pointed to the fact that trade between African countries is primarily driven by manufactured goods, which account for 45 per cent of intra-African commerce, compared to just 20 per cent of the continent’s exports outside Africa.
In terms of the auto industry, Stellantis South African and sub-Saharan African head, Mike Whitfield – who will one of the speakers at the automotive conference – announced at a recent Stellantis event in Johannesburg proper implementation of the AfCFTA combined with the growing number of automotive assembly plants in Africa could see countries – including South Africa – importing vehicles from within Africa in the near future. However, she was frank about the challenges, noting that intra-African trade still represents a mere 15 per cent of total African trade. She identified systemic barriers, including costly trade restrictions, fragmented infrastructure and financial systems that do not connect, which make trading with a neighbour more difficult than trading abroad.
Wamkele Mene, Secretary General of the AfCFTA Secretariat, added: “The AfCFTA is already delivering. Intra-African trade rebounded strongly in 2024, recording a 12.4 per cent increase from 2023, according to
Afreximbank’s African Trade Report 2025. This recovery underscores growing confidence in Africa’s integration model under the AfCFTA.
Beyond the headline figures, the data shows a gradual shift in the continent’s trade composition. While primary commodities still dominate, there is a clear growth in machinery, motor vehicles, food products, chemicals and electronics. This shift signals our continent’s transition from raw commodity dependency toward industrial diversification, a shift that will only be sustained by stronger logistics and manufacturing value chains.

a3579.t:
- For more financial news,go to the News24 Business front page.
US president Donald Trump's administration on Wednesday ordered the closure of a US agency that invested billions in African and other developing countries' infrastructure in return for good governance, effectively ceding ground to China.
The Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) will immediately exit projects around the world, from building roads to modernizing electricity grids, likely leaving the works under construction unless other partners step in.
An MCC executive at a staff meeting on Wednesday told staff that "we are coming to an orderly close" with all programs to be discontinued, according to an employee who was present.
The meeting came after a staff-wide memo, seen by AFP, informed that billionaire Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency was imposing a "significant reduction" at MCC and laid out practicalities for the majority of staff who will lose jobs.
Founded in 2004 under former president George W. Bush with bipartisan support, MCC signs contracts for US investment in developing countries that meet standards on economic transparency and good governance.
MCC has since invested $17 billion with numerous prominent projects underway.
Just in October, Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema - who has consolidated democracy at home - vowed to keep upholding "shared values" with the United States as he signed a half-billion-dollar agreement to improve roads, irrigation and electricity.
Trump has made clear he has limited interest in sub-Saharan Africa and that he opposes development aid, which he sees as not directly benefiting the United States, earlier shuttering the US Agency for International Development, a much larger government body.
The MCC employee, speaking on condition of anonymity to avoid retribution, said the organization differed significantly from USAID.
"We're not doing humanitarian assistance. We're not doing social justice. We're very much building up an environment for private-sector investment in foreign economies," she told AFP.
"This is a very different thing, something that actually does put America first," she said.
"It's interesting, if we're worried about China's influence in the world, that we would shutter MCC, which builds large-scale infrastructure that counters China's influence."
Area of competition with China
Infrastructure projects - roads, hospitals and other buildings - have been a signature selling point for China, which the United States sees as its primary adversary.
Chinese President Xi Jinping in September vowed another $51 billion of investment in Africa over the next three years.
The United States under former president Joe Biden acknowledged it cannot keep up with such high-profile, state-led spending but argued it can offer a more sustainable model.
MCC will inform countries on Friday that compacts will be terminated within 40 days, the staffer said.
After negotiations with Musk's team, MCC was allowed extensions in four countries -- Ivory Coast, Mongolia, Nepal and Senegal.
In Nepal, Mongolia and Senegal, the MCC will have up to three months, with hopes of making construction sites safe.
The goal is "so someone is not going to fall into a pit or something," the employee said. "Whether or not we'll be successful, I don't know."
MCC was granted slightly longer in Ivory Coast where the project, which includes support for integrating major road arteries, is nearing completion.
The Nepal project was sealed in 2022 despite street protests against it by leftists in Kathmandu.
The $500 million grant in China's small Himalayan neighbor aims to improve roads and increase cross-border electricity trading with US-friendly India.
In Senegal, a $600 million initiative - $550 million from MCC and $50 million from the Senegalese government - has included ramping up electricity outside urban areas.
Elizabeth Hoffman, executive director for North America at ONE, the anti-poverty group co-founded by Bono, voiced alarm at the shutdown.
"MCC brings an innovative and entrepreneurial approach to development assistance that holds governments accountable and effectively counters malign foreign influences like China," she said.
MCC and Trump administration did not immediately comment on the cuts, which were first reported by development specialist site Devex.

a3674.t:
Le président de la Chambre de Commerce de Djibouti, Youssouf Moussa Dawaleh et l’ambassadeur des Etats-Unis, Larry E. André ont conjointement présidé le jeudi 16 juillet dernier, la cérémonie de remise de certificat de la première promotion de conducteurs de véhicules de transport routier de marchandise, formé par le Centre de Ressources et de Compétences des métiers portuaires (CRC). Organisé par la CCD en collaboration avec l’AFD et l’USAID, l’événement qui s’inscrit dans le cadre du projet d’amélioration de l’employabilité de la main d’œuvre locale, vise à répondre aux besoins du marché de l’emploi.
Une vingtaine de bénéficiaire d’un stage de formation de conducteur de véhicule de transport routier, étaient le jeudi dernier, dans la salle de conférence de la chambre de commerce de Djibouti, sous les crépitements et flashs des cameras des professionnels des médias nationaux. Et pour cause, ils ont reçu des mains respectives, de l’ambassadeur des Etats-Unis d’Amérique, accrédité à Djibouti, Larry E. André, du président de la Chambre du commerce de Djibouti, Youssouf Moussa Dawaleh, du directeur de l’Agence Française de Développement (AFD), Philippe Collignon, du représentant adjoint de l’USAID sous nos cieux, Alpha S. Diallo, de la représentante résidente du système des Nations Unies, Barbara Manzi, de la cheffe du projet ‘‘Education Development Center’’ de l’USAID, Laura Dillon-Binkley, du directeur du département ‘‘Transports’’ du ministère de l’équipement et des transports (MET), Dileita Sultan Mohamed et du président du conseil d’administration du centre de Ressources et de Compétences de métiers portuaires (CRC), Abdi Farah, les certificats validant leur aptitude à conduire tous les types de véhicules, dont notamment ceux du transport routier de marchandise.
Organisé par la chambre de commerce de Djibouti (CCD) en collaboration avec l’Agence Française de développement (AFD) et celle des Etats Unis pour le Développement International (USAID), cet événement qui s’inscrit dans le cadre du Projet d’Employabilité de la main-d’œuvre de Djibouti (PED), est venu couronner 4 semaines d’une formation sur les compétences de bases en employabilité et en entrepreneuriat (CBEE) au sein de l’Education Development Center, et des cours pratiques dispensé par des professionnels du centre de Ressources et de Compétences de métiers portuaires (CRC).
A noter que le PED est un projet quinquennal financé par le gouvernement des États-Unis par l’intermédiaire de l’Agence des États-Unis pour le développement international (USAID). Lequel vise selon ses concepteurs, à améliorer les compétences et la compétitivité des demandeurs d’emploi djiboutiens en conformité avec les normes internationaux. Le détail laisse entrevoir les exigences réelles du marché du travail dans le domaine des transports routiers.
Lors de la cérémonie de jeudi, le président de la chambre de commerce de Djibouti, Youssouf Moussa Dawaleh a, dans un discours prononcé à cette occasion, déclaré que les financements mobilisés dans le cadre de ce projet, ont permis la formation de jeunes chercheurs d’emplois, dans les métiers en cohérence avec la vision du développement économique de Djibouti, à savoir le transport, et la logistique portuaire.
«Pour cela, un accord cadre a été signé entre le Centre de Ressources et de Compétences et EDC/USAID, afin de former 400 jeunes chercheurs d’emplois, aux métiers portuaire, transports et logistiques, et ce pour répondre aux besoins du marché du travail» a-t-il ajouté avant d’exhorter les entreprises opérants dans ce domaine, à ses rapprocher du CRC pour s’informer sur les compétences des jeunes formés dans les normes reconnus dans le monde.
De son côté, le chef de la chancellerie américaine de notre pays, Larry E. André, a indiqué que le partenariat tripartite tissé pour cette occasion, entre la CCD, l’AFD et l’USAID, a abouti à la mise en place d’une formation de haut niveau dans le domaine des transports et de la logistique destinée à des jeunes insuffisamment scolarisés qui selon le diplomate américain représentent une couche importante des jeunes demandeurs d’emploi. «Je saisi cette occasion pour vous rassurer de la disponibilité du peuple américain à travers l’USAID à poursuivre le financement à hauteur de 50% du cout de la formation jusqu’à l’atteinte de la cible des 400 jeunes dans le cadre de ce partenariat» a-t-il dit à ses partenaires.
Sur ce, les officiels ont remis à chacun des lauréats les certificats internationaux qui leurs permettraient à conduire tous les types de véhicules aussi bien à l’intérieur qu’à l’extérieur de notre pays.
Rachid Bayleh
La parole à…Larry E. André,
Ambassadeur des Etats Unis
«Le gouvernement des USA, renouvelle son engagement pour soutenir Djibouti dans ses efforts de développer le capital humain dans le cadre de la vision 2035»
Ces formations ont été rendues possibles, grâce au partenariat tripartite entre la Chambre de Commerce de Djibouti, l’Agence Française de Développement et l’Agence des Etats Unis pour le Développement International (USAID). En effet, ce partenariat entre les trois institutions permet de répondre à la demande croissante de personnels qualifiés dans le secteur privé, ce qui appuie les efforts déployés par le Gouvernement pour créer des emplois et favoriser le recrutement des jeunes et des femmes plus particulièrement dans les secteurs de la logistique et du transport. Djibouti fait face aux deux défis liés d’une part, au manque de candidats qualifiés pour des postes techniques disponibles chez les employeurs et d’autre part au manque d’opportunités pour les jeunes et les femmes d’être embauchés. La formation technique répond aux deux défis à la fois. Le gouvernement des Etats-Unis d’Amérique renouvelle son engagement de soutenir le gouvernement de la République de Djibouti dans ses efforts louables de développer le capital humain dans le cadre de la vision 2035.
Le point avec…Youssouf Moussa Dawaleh
Président de la Chambre de Commerce de Djibouti
« La Chambre de Commerce de Djibouti a souhaité créer des synergies entre les projets dans lesquels elle intervient »
Notre institution, en qualité de représentante du secteur privé à Djibouti, est une des parties prenantes de ce projet qui vise à rehausser les capacités et stimuler l’employabilité et l’entrepreneuriat des jeunes et des demandeurs d’emploi dans notre pays. Et ce, aux cotés de partenaires institutionnels tels que le Ministère du Travail, à travers l’ANEFIP, le Ministère de l’Education Nationale et bien sûr le Ministère des Transports. La Chambre de Commerce de Djibouti a souhaité créer des synergies entre les projets dans lesquels elle intervient. Il est donc prévu de les formes à la conduite des véhicules articulés et porteurs, des bus pour le transport en commun, des RTG, RS et des portiques ainsi que des chariots élévateurs. A ce jour, 100 personnes ont été formées, 78 pour les véhicules articulés pour les détenteurs de permis E et 22 pour les véhicules porteurs, pour les titulaires de permis C. Nous faisons malheureusement face à la difficulté de mobiliser suffisamment des personnes répondant au pré requis pour la conduite de véhicules articulés qui doivent être titulaires de permis E. Nous nous sommes, à cet effet, rapprochés de plusieurs partenaires afin de faciliter l’obtention des permis E aux jeunes chômeurs et leur permettre d’intégrer la formation. Nous espérons résoudre cette question au plut tôt, et saisissons l’occasion de cette cérémonie pour informer le plus grand nombre de cette problématique. En effet, dans le contexte économique actuel, en pleine mutation, il convient pour toute personne de saisir toutes les opportunités qui se présentent afin d’accroître ses connaissances et compétences. Etant entendu que la formation professionnelle est un accélérateur de carrière et un tremplin pour un meilleur avenir professionnel.
Ils ont dit… Laura Dillon-Binkley
Cheffe du projet ‘‘Education Development Center’’ de l’USAID
«Le CRC va assurer la formation de demandeurs d’emplois djiboutiens qualifiés qui peuvent s’insérer dans l’emploi avec succès»
«Je tiens à remercié la chambre de commerce et tous les bailleurs de fonds, l’Union Européenne, l’Agence française pour le développement, l’USAID et le gouvernement américain pour la mise en place de ce centre vraiment d’important capitale pour Djibouti en ce qui concerne la formation technique des métiers portuaires. Parce qu’on sait qu’il y a une indication avec le profil cherché par les employeurs dans les ports et la disponibilité sur le marché de personnes qualifiées. Et ce centre de formation va combler cette lacune et assurer qu’on a des demandeurs d’emplois djiboutiens, qui sont qualifiés et qui peuvent s’insérer dans l’emploi avec succès»
Mohamed Ahmed Houssein
Bénéficiaire de la formation
«Cette formation m’a servi de me perfectionner et de maitriser la conduite de tous les types de véhicules»
«Malgré mes années d’expériences en qualité de chauffeur de camion, auparavant je ne pouvais pas répondre aux exigences des entreprises internationaux qui opèrent dans nos différentes infrastructures portuaires. Cette formation m’a servi de me perfectionner et de maitriser la conduite de tous les types de véhicules. Ces 4 semaines de formations m’ont servi d’apprendre beaucoup appris en ce qui concerne à communiquer la communication interpersonnelle, le fait d’être proactif vis-à-vis d’une situation quelconque et de travailler dans un esprit d’équipe avec ses collaborateurs. Avec le certificat que j’ai eu aujourd’hui, je vais trouver un emploi bien rémunéré. Je profite de cette occasion pour remercier le CRC, l’EDC, l’AFD, l’USAID et le CCD. Je remercie également le président de la république Ismail Omar Guelleh et la première dame Kadra Mahamoud Haid pour sa politique de développer du capital humain qui nous a permis de prendre part à cette formation qui certes relèvera notre niveau de vie»
Propos recueillis par RB
a3674.en:
Djiboutian Workforce Employability Project: Certificates awarded to road freight vehicle drivers

The President of the Djibouti Chamber of Commerce, Youssouf Moussa Dawaleh, and the United States Ambassador, Larry E. Andre, jointly presided on Thursday, 16 July, over the ceremony awarding certificates to the first cohort of road freight vehicle drivers trained by the Centre for Port Trades Resources and Skills (CRC). Organised by the CCD in collaboration with the AFD and USAID, the event, which falls within the framework of the project to improve the employability of the local workforce, aims to respond to the needs of the labour market.

Some twenty beneficiaries of a training course for road freight vehicle drivers were, last Thursday, in the conference room of the Djibouti Chamber of Commerce, under the clicking and flashing cameras of national media professionals. And for good reason: they received, from the hands respectively of the Ambassador of the United States of America accredited to Djibouti, Larry E. Andre; the President of the Djibouti Chamber of Commerce, Youssouf Moussa Dawaleh; the Director of the French Development Agency (AFD), Philippe Collignon; the Deputy Representative of USAID in our country, Alpha S. Diallo; the UN system Resident Representative, Barbara Manzi; the head of USAID's "Education Development Center" project, Laura Dillon-Binkley; the Director of the "Transport" department of the Ministry of Equipment and Transport (MET), Dileita Sultan Mohamed; and the Chairman of the Board of the Centre for Port Trades Resources and Skills (CRC), Abdi Farah, the certificates validating their ability to drive all types of vehicles, including in particular those used for road freight transport.

Organised by the Djibouti Chamber of Commerce (CCD) in collaboration with the French Development Agency (AFD) and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), this event, part of the Djibouti Workforce Employability Project (PED), capped four weeks of training in basic employability and entrepreneurship skills (CBEE) at the Education Development Center, and practical courses delivered by professionals from the Centre for Port Trades Resources and Skills (CRC).

It should be noted that the PED is a five-year project financed by the United States government through the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). According to its designers, it aims to improve the skills and competitiveness of Djiboutian jobseekers in line with international standards. The details point to the real requirements of the labour market in the road transport field.

At Thursday's ceremony, the President of the Djibouti Chamber of Commerce, Youssouf Moussa Dawaleh, said in a speech delivered for the occasion that the funding mobilised under this project had made it possible to train young jobseekers in trades consistent with Djibouti's vision of economic development, namely transport and port logistics.

"To that end, a framework agreement has been signed between the Centre for Resources and Skills and EDC/USAID, in order to train 400 young jobseekers in port, transport and logistics trades, so as to meet the needs of the labour market," he added, before urging companies operating in this field to get in touch with the CRC to learn about the skills of the young people trained to internationally recognised standards.

For his part, the head of the American chancellery in our country, Larry E. Andre, indicated that the tripartite partnership woven for this occasion between the CCD, the AFD and USAID had resulted in the establishment of high-level training in the field of transport and logistics for young people with insufficient schooling, who according to the American diplomat represent a large share of young jobseekers. "I take this opportunity to assure you of the readiness of the American people, through USAID, to continue financing 50% of the cost of the training until the target of 400 young people is reached under this partnership," he told his partners.

With that, the officials handed each of the graduates the international certificates that would allow them to drive all types of vehicles both inside and outside our country.

Rachid Bayleh

A word from... Larry E. Andre, Ambassador of the United States
"The US government renews its commitment to support Djibouti in its efforts to develop human capital within the framework of Vision 2035"

These training courses were made possible thanks to the tripartite partnership between the Djibouti Chamber of Commerce, the French Development Agency and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). Indeed, this partnership between the three institutions makes it possible to respond to the growing demand for qualified personnel in the private sector, which supports the efforts made by the Government to create jobs and promote the hiring of young people and women, particularly in the logistics and transport sectors. Djibouti faces two linked challenges: on the one hand the lack of qualified candidates for technical positions available with employers, and on the other the lack of opportunities for young people and women to be hired. Technical training addresses both challenges at once. The government of the United States of America renews its commitment to support the government of the Republic of Djibouti in its laudable efforts to develop human capital within the framework of Vision 2035.

An update with... Youssouf Moussa Dawaleh, President of the Djibouti Chamber of Commerce
"The Djibouti Chamber of Commerce wanted to create synergies among the projects in which it is involved"

Our institution, as the representative of the private sector in Djibouti, is one of the stakeholders in this project, which aims to raise capacities and stimulate the employability and entrepreneurship of young people and jobseekers in our country. And this alongside institutional partners such as the Ministry of Labour, through ANEFIP, the Ministry of National Education and of course the Ministry of Transport. The Djibouti Chamber of Commerce wanted to create synergies among the projects in which it is involved. It is therefore planned to train them in driving articulated and rigid vehicles, buses for public transport, RTGs, RSs and gantry cranes as well as forklifts. To date, 100 people have been trained: 78 for articulated vehicles for holders of category E licences and 22 for rigid vehicles, for holders of category C licences. Unfortunately, we face the difficulty of mobilising enough people meeting the prerequisites for driving articulated vehicles, who must hold a category E licence. To this end, we have approached several partners in order to facilitate the obtaining of category E licences for young unemployed people and allow them to join the training. We hope to resolve this question as soon as possible, and we take the opportunity of this ceremony to inform as many people as possible of this problem. Indeed, in the current economic context, which is in full transformation, it is appropriate for everyone to seize every opportunity that arises in order to increase their knowledge and skills. It being understood that vocational training is a career accelerator and a springboard to a better professional future.

They said... Laura Dillon-Binkley, Head of USAID's "Education Development Center" project
"The CRC will provide training for qualified Djiboutian jobseekers who can successfully enter employment"

"I want to thank the chamber of commerce and all the donors, the European Union, the French Development Agency, USAID and the American government for the establishment of this centre, which is truly of capital importance for Djibouti with regard to technical training in port trades. Because we know that there is a mismatch between the profile sought by employers in the ports and the availability on the market of qualified people. And this training centre will fill that gap and ensure that we have Djiboutian jobseekers who are qualified and who can successfully enter employment."

Mohamed Ahmed Houssein, training beneficiary
"This training helped me improve and master the driving of all types of vehicles"

"Despite my years of experience as a truck driver, previously I could not meet the requirements of the international companies that operate in our various port facilities. This training helped me improve and master the driving of all types of vehicles. These 4 weeks of training helped me learn a great deal about interpersonal communication, being proactive in any given situation and working in a spirit of teamwork with one's colleagues. With the certificate I received today, I will find a well-paid job. I take this opportunity to thank the CRC, the EDC, the AFD, USAID and the CCD. I also thank the President of the Republic Ismail Omar Guelleh and the First Lady Kadra Mahamoud Haid for her policy of developing human capital, which allowed us to take part in this training which will certainly raise our standard of living."

Interviews by RB

a3685.t:
DODOMA: THE government has successfully reviewed its 2024/2025 budget and secured over 220bn/- to cover critical areas affected by recent shifts in United States foreign aid policy.
Finance Minister, Dr Mwigulu Nchemba, informed the National Assembly yesterday that 88bn/- of the funds have already been disbursed to ensure the continuation of key health projects impacted by the policy changes.
He was responding to a supplementary question from Patrick Ndakidemi (CCM), MP for Moshi Rural, who inquired about the effect of a recent executive order by former US President Donald Trump on development initiatives in Tanzania and how the country plans to utilise its natural resources to mitigate such external shocks.
Dr Nchemba clarified that Tanzania had no direct government-to-government financial cooperation with the US for development project funding. Instead, most US development assistance was channelled through American institutions working with Tanzanian partners.
“There was no direct budgetary impact following the foreign aid policy changes,” he said, adding, “However, the government conducted a thorough assessment of institutions previously receiving such funds — not only in response to the US policy shift but as part of a broader review of support from development partners.”
He said the government is committed to ensuring continuity of the affected projects, especially in the health sector, by allocating necessary funds from its own budget and other sources.
ALSO READ: US aid agency is in upheaval during foreign assistance freeze and staff departures
Beyond responding to aid shortfalls, Dr Nchemba said the government is intensifying efforts to operationalise major domestic projects that rely on locally available resources to boost domestic revenue and reduce reliance on imported goods.
“These initiatives will not only generate substantial income but also increase the production of goods that can be made locally, enhancing economic resilience,” he noted.
Responding to Ndakidemi’s primary question on the government’s preparedness to counter foreign policy shifts from developed nations, Dr Nchemba said Tanzania is scaling up efforts to increase domestic revenue generation, aiming to finance a significant portion of the national budget internally.
He added that the government will continue to attract private sector participation in development financing through publicprivate partnerships (PPPs) and other innovative models.
“This strategy will help reduce the borrowing burden on the government and lessen budgetary dependence on development partners,” he said.

a3718.t:
L'ONU suspend l'aide alimentaire en Afrique de l'Ouest et Centrale en raison de coupes budgétaires
Face à l'épuisement de ses fonds, le PAM suspend ses opérations en cours dans sept pays dont la Mauritanie, le Mali et la République centrafricaine, où les stocks alimentaires ne devraient durer que quelques semaines.
Le Programme alimentaire mondial (PAM) a annoncé vendredi qu'il suspendait son aide alimentaire et nutritionnelle dans les pays d'Afrique de l'Ouest et centrale touchés par des crises, en raison des réductions de l'aide américaine, ce qui paralyse les opérations de l'organisation.
Bien que les délais varient, les stocks alimentaires devraient suffire jusqu'à environ septembre pour la plupart des pays concernés, laissant potentiellement des millions de personnes vulnérables sans aucune aide d'urgence, selon le PAM.
« Nous faisons tout notre possible pour prioriser les activités les plus vitales, mais sans un soutien urgent de nos partenaires, notre capacité de réponse diminue chaque jour. Nous avons besoin d'un financement durable pour maintenir l'approvisionnement alimentaire et garder l'espoir vivant », a déclaré Margot van der Velden, directrice régionale du PAM, à l'Associated Press.
Sept pays de la région sont concernés, avec une suspension des opérations déjà en cours en Mauritanie, au Mali et en République centrafricaine, où les stocks alimentaires ne devraient durer que quelques semaines.
Des millions de personnes affectées
La distribution d'aide a déjà été considérablement réduite dans les camps camerounais accueillant des réfugiés nigérians, selon le PAM.
Des millions de personnes devraient être immédiatement affectées, selon les données du PAM consultées par l'AP, y compris 300 000 enfants au Nigeria exposés à un risque de « malnutrition sévère, augmentant finalement le risque de décès ».
Le PAM indique qu'il a besoin de 494 millions de dollars pour couvrir la seconde moitié de 2025, mais les fonds sont totalement épuisés, le forçant à prioriser les groupes les plus vulnérables. Dans le nord et le centre du Mali, il privilégiera les réfugiés nouvellement déplacés et les enfants de moins de cinq ans.
a3718.en:
The UN suspends food aid in West and Central Africa because of budget cuts

Faced with the exhaustion of its funds, the WFP is suspending its ongoing operations in seven countries including Mauritania, Mali and the Central African Republic, where food stocks are expected to last only a few weeks.

The World Food Programme (WFP) announced on Friday that it was suspending its food and nutrition aid in crisis-affected countries of West and Central Africa because of cuts in American aid, which is paralysing the organisation's operations.

Although the timelines vary, food stocks should be sufficient until around September for most of the countries concerned, potentially leaving millions of vulnerable people without any emergency assistance, according to the WFP.

"We are doing everything we can to prioritise the most life-saving activities, but without urgent support from our partners, our response capacity diminishes every day. We need sustainable funding to maintain the food supply and keep hope alive," said Margot van der Velden, WFP Regional Director, to the Associated Press.

Seven countries in the region are affected, with a suspension of operations already under way in Mauritania, Mali and the Central African Republic, where food stocks are expected to last only a few weeks.

Millions of people affected

Aid distribution has already been considerably reduced in the Cameroonian camps hosting Nigerian refugees, according to the WFP.

Millions of people are expected to be immediately affected, according to WFP data consulted by the AP, including 300,000 children in Nigeria exposed to a risk of "severe malnutrition, ultimately increasing the risk of death."

The WFP indicates that it needs 494 million dollars to cover the second half of 2025, but the funds are completely exhausted, forcing it to prioritise the most vulnerable groups. In northern and central Mali, it will give priority to newly displaced refugees and children under five.

a3763.t:
There are lingering questions on the Director of Public Prosecution’s (DPP) exercise of power to prosecute or discontinue cases, with experts calling for more transparency and accountability.
Speaking at a seminar organised by Youth and Society (YAS) in Lilongwe on Thursday to reflect on the office of the DPP, stakeholders who included lawyers, economists and governance commentators said there is need for detailed regulation on how the DPP exercises power.
In his presentation, Malawi Law Society (MLS) vice-president Tusume Mwabungulu proposed that the DPP’s decisions to discontinue cases must be reviewed by the courts.
He said: “DPPs reasons for exercise of powers must be reviewable by the courts. There must be more transparency and accountability.”
Mwabungulu said there is need to develop detailed regulations on how to exercise these powers to allay public fears on what considerations have been made.
Under Section 99 of the Constitution sub-Section 2 (a and b), the DPP is mandated to “take over and continue any criminal proceedings” which have been instituted or undertaken by any other person or authority, and further “to discontinue at any stage before judgement is delivered any criminal proceedings instituted or undertaken by himself or herself or any other person or authority”.
In her paper reflecting on the implication of the DPP’s conduct to the economy, University of Malawi economist Bertha Bangara-Chikadza said the exercise of power for this office can boost or kill the economy.
She said: “In cases involving cross-border crimes such as money laundering, human trafficking, or cybercrime, the DPP’s actions can have international economic implications.
“Cooperation with foreign jurisdictions and adherence to global standards can enhance a country’s reputation and attract foreign investment.”
Bangara-Chikadza, who is also Economists Association of Malawi president, added that failure to prosecute such crimes effectively may “lead to sanctions, reduced foreign aid, or exclusion from international financial systems”, all of which may hurt the economy.
In a joint paper, activist Benedicto Kondowe and political scientist Ernest Thindwa recommended the establishment of a prosecutorial oversight committee within Parliament that should periodically review the DPP’s performance.
The two also proposed strengthening the parliamentary Legal Affairs Committee’s oversight mandate to scrutinise the basis of discontinuance beyond merely providing reasons as required under Section 99 of the Constitution.
In his welcoming remarks, YAS executive director Charles Kajoloweka said the DPP sits at the heart of the justice system; hence, the need for improved accountability.
“But history has shown that this office, like many others, is not immune to political pressure, resource constraints, and systemic inefficiencies.
“The question we must answer today is: how do we transform the DPP’s mandate into a beacon of accountability rather than an instrument of political convenience?” he said.
Kajoloweka said they will compile the suggestions from the seminar and present them to authorities for consideration.
Responding to the concerns, DPP Masauko Chamkakala said the office follows to the letter the accountability mechanism provided under the law.

* Introduction
Before dealing with substantive issues raised by the Minister in the Budget Speech, I wish to raise certain general issues some of which I did raise last year but were not satisfactorily responded to. The first one is that of the huge foreign exchange reserves that we keep in foreign banks. While it is understandable both for the purpose of financing the import of goods and services and for reasons of economic prudence that substantial foreign exchange reserves should always be kept, it does not seem to make any economic sense to keep such excessive amounts of money idle in foreign banks. The huge challenges of development that we face necessitate the use of at least part of funds to finance development projects or for productive investment.
