a4012.t:
South Africa will lead the next refunding exercise for the Global Fund, raising money for the international partnership fighting AIDS after the US cut healthcare support to the continent.
Winnie Byanyima, executive director of the Joint United Nations Program on HIV/AIDS, announced South African President Cyril Ramaphosa’s agreement to take charge of the upcoming three-year funding cycle at a press conference in Johannesburg on Friday.
AIDS “is very much an African disease now, with 75% of people living with HIV being on this continent,” she told reporters.
“The Global Fund replenishment is critical and it’s great that South Africa has offered to lead that,” she said.
The Fund, an independent partnership where money mainly comes from public sector donors, plans to raise at least $18 billion as it launches its 2026-2028 fundraising cycle. Success of the exercise will be crucial for expanding efforts to combat HIV, tuberculosis and malaria, and to strengthen health systems.
As it is, a smaller amount of foreign aid means a plan to end the disease as a public health threat by 2030 “will get more and more off-track,” Byanyima said.
The replenishment is expected to happen in South Africa in September.
While poor African countries are working hard to fill the sudden gap created by President Donald Trump’s decision to halt US aid, they are going to have to do more with less, she said. There was also an urgent need to restructure their debts to cut debt-service costs that can be many times larger than their healthcare budgets, she added.
UNAIDS is also working with South Africa, the country with the largest number of people infected with HIV, to help it make better use of its resources and ensure that vital community-led monitoring programs aren’t lost.
“South Africa is a leader and the region itself has been making progress and can continue making progress in spite of the funding freeze by the American government,” Byanyima said.
But it “needs to move faster on reducing new infections,” and ensuring key at-risk communities including migrants, men who have sex with men, sex workers and drug users have appropriate services.

a4100.t:
Despite the suspension of its activities in Djibo, the French relief organisation gave assurances that it will continue to offer its services in other regions of Burkina Faso.
Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) announced on Monday, October 21, 2024, the suspension of its activities in the city of Djibo, located in the north of Burkina Faso.
The NGO said it took the decision following repeated incidents targeting health centers, water distribution points and its premises.
“We need adequate security conditions to allow our teams to continue their mission and provide assistance to communities affected by insecurity and violence,” said Dr. Moussa Ousman, MSF’s program manager.
However, MSF gave assurances that its teams will continue to provide humanitarian assistance in other regions of the country.
In the first half of this year, MSF workers were able to provide 348,477 consultations, care for 3,127 mental health patients, and distribute 71,993,500 liters of water.
“We hope that the security situation will improve, giving us better guarantees for the protection of our teams and our activities, so that we can resume our assistance to Djibouti,” added Dr. Moussa Ousman.
In February, two MSF staff were killed in an attack on a clearly marked MSF vehicle carrying a four-man medical team.
Ds/sf/ac/lb/as/APA

a4192.t:
C’est le titre du dernier et deuxième long métrage de Sylvestre Amoussou, sorti ce mercredi 9 novembre 2011 en France, et à l’affiche à l’espace Saint Michel de Paris. ‘Un pas en avant, les dessous de la corruption’ est un polar politique dans lequel s’enchaînent enquête, péripéties, suspenses, poursuites et meurtres. Un polar qui traite, avec légèreté, d’un sujet universel grave, celui de la corruption et de l’aide humanitaire mondiale, elle, allègrement détournée tant en aval qu’en amont par les acteurs censés en administrer la gestion. Sylvestre Amoussou y relate justement l’histoire d’un petit artisan à la recherche de son frère.
Et qui se retrouve finalement embarqué dans une affaire de détournement d’aide humanitaire… Les principaux acteurs que sont : Thierry Desroses, Dieudonné Kabongo, Firmine Richard, Fatou N’Diaye sont venus de France où ils étaient habitués à jouer des rôles secondaires. Le réalisateur et la production du film n’ont pas lésiné sur les moyens en faisant venir au Bénin d’autres acteurs secondaires du Sénégal et des Antilles et des techniciens français. Des rôles secondaires et de figurants ont été réservés aux acteurs locaux. A l’exception de Sandra Adjaho, actrice-interprète béninoise et résidente au Bénin, qui hérita, à la faveur d’un casting époustouflant, du premier rôle féminin, Délali Godomey la femme du personnage principal. Un rôle qu’elle a su illuminer de sa beauté naturelle et tout son talent d’actrice confirmée. Sylvestre Amoussou incarne lui-même, en déployant son immense talent d’acteur, avec gravité et parfois une fine candeur, le personnage principal Koffi Godomey ; ce qui lui a valu le prix de la meilleure interprétation masculine au Fespaco et aux ‘Ecrans noirs’ du Cameroun. Le film décrochera aussi d’autres prix, tel que le prix de la meilleure musique au Fespaco, etc.
Ce film tourné, dans des décors intérieurs et des décors naturels très pittoresques africains, se veut le témoin-projecteur de l’image d’une Afrique rayonnante, loin des clichés misérabilistes des fléaux dévastateurs, des conflits et des catastrophes surmédiatisées facturés par les occidentaux.
Le tournage du film a entièrement eu lieu au Bénin. Le décor et les paysages magnifient les villes de Cotonou, Abomey-Calavi, et subliment également les éco-systèmes des environs de la Cité lacustre de Ganvié, avec de magnifiques mangroves’, filmées sous un angle nouveau jamais réalisé jusque-lors, avec d’incroyables plans aériens !…
Sylvestre Amoussou, nous allons bientôt vivre la sortie du film «Un pas en avant, les dessous de la corruption» en France. Quels sont les messages que vous véhiculez à travers cette œuvre ?
Sylvestre Amoussou : A travers mon film le message principal concerne la lutte contre la corruption.
Corruption qui existe aussi bien au sommet de l’Etat, qu’au niveau du citoyen de base.
« UN PAS EN AVANT – Les Dessous de la Corruption » ne peut pas à lui seul changer la situation africaine, mais mon intention principale est de susciter chez le spectateur l’envie de se battre contre la corruption, de prendre part aux élections locales, faisant ainsi un pas vers la démocratie.
Dans ce film, je redonne également sa place à la femme. Sans les femmes, l’homme n’est rien. Et je pense qu’avec plus de femmes aux postes suprêmes il y aurait moins de guerre. Une femme pense toujours à l’avenir de ses enfants et donc à l’avenir de son pays.
L’Assemblée nationale béninoise a adopté le 29 Août dernier le projet de loi contre la corruption et les infractions connexes en République du Bénin. «Un pas en avant, les dessous de la corruption» a bénéficié d’une aide du gouvernement béninois. Tout ceci augure d’une bonne volonté de prise de conscience du fléau par les autorités béninoises. Ne projetez-vous pas une collaboration avec les autorités gouvernementales pour la diffusion du film au Bénin ?
Sylvestre Amoussou : J’espère que ce ne sera pas une loi de plus qui ne sera pas appliquée. Je suis allé vers le gouvernement pour qu’il organise une projection au BENIN, pour le moment c’est toujours lettre morte. Je le déplore car je pense que le gouvernement ne donne pas une place assez importante au cinéma qui peut développer humainement et économiquement un pays. Face à la mondialisation, et à l’ère d’internet le gouvernement n’a pas pris toute l’importance de posséder et contrôler son image aussi bien au niveau national qu’international. Mais je ne désespère pas, bien au contraire.
Les dessous de la corruption, comme l’indique le titre, est un film sur la corruption. Qu’est-ce qui fait son originalité ?
Sylvestre Amoussou : Sa plus grande originalité : son mode de financement. En effet, la majorité des fonds vient aussi bien de la société civile africaine que des politiques africains qui commencent à comprendre que seule l’image qu’ils financent peut restituer une image positive du continent. Même si le film critique la société africaine actuelle, il dessine une Afrique moderne, belle et qui gagne. Cette image ne sera jamais financée par l’occident.
Réaliser un film nécessite beaucoup de moyens financiers. Comment avez-vous financez le vôtre, tout en conservant cette originalité qui vous est très chère ?
Sylvestre Amoussou : J’ai été soutenu par le gouvernement du Bénin, la société civile béninoise, le fonds de France indépendant qui a apporté un apport de 70 000 euros et le centre du cinéma marocain. Le film est totalement indépendant. Je suis libre de dire ce que bon me semble. C’est très important, car il n’est pas biaisé ni orienté. La plupart des films africains sont financés par la France. Ce qui est problématique puisqu’elle veut en retour qu’on parle d’elle selon son point de vue. D’ailleurs, les médias français comme France télévisions, refusent de parler de ce film car ils ne veulent pas apporter de l’importance à un film qui met en cause les relations que la France entretient avec l’Afrique. Peu de salles de cinéma ont accepté de le diffuser. Seul le dirigeant de l’espace Saint Michel à Paris a accepté de le diffuser car il s’est basé sur la qualité du film tout simplement. Nous espérons que le public l’aimera pour qu’il soit diffusé dans d’autres salles.
Parfait ! Ainsi quelques institutions et de diverses personnalités au Bénin et ailleurs en Afrique, donc des gens parfaitement intègres, mais aussi certainement quelques corrompus et corrupteurs, vous ont soutenu pour la réalisation de ce film. Peut-on y voir le signe d’un acte d’espoir en pensant à certains, et un acte de repentance en pensant à d’autres de vos financiers qui traînent eux des casseroles en la matière ?
Sylvestre Amoussou : En tout cas je l’espère. Mais il est vrai qu’il y a toute une éducation à refaire car le colon a bien ancré la corruption dans nos civilisations et certains africains se l’ont totalement appropriée et même sont devenus maître en la matière. Nos dialectes ne possèdent pas le mot « corruption ». La langue française oui ! Et n’oublions pas que pour qu’il y ait des corrompus il faut à la base des corrupteurs.
On a vu que certains membres du gouvernement du pays, théâtre du film, étaient ‘ hyper-corrompus’, notamment le Premier Ministre. Ne craignez-vous pas une confusion possible avec les membres du gouvernement béninois vue que le film a été entièrement tourné au Bénin ?
Sylvestre Amoussou : Non. Le film a été effectivement entièrement tourné au Bénin, c’est un choix juste de mise en valeur de notre pays, à travers ces beaux paysages et son effort infrastructurel pour se mettre à niveau des normes touristiques internationales. Le pays théâtre du film reste les Etats-Unis d’Afrique. Vous voyez bien d’ailleurs que son drapeau est une bannière étoilée représentant l’ensemble des Etats africains. Il n’y a, non plus, aucune confusion possible entre le premier ministre actuel du BENIN et le premier ministre corrompu de mon film. Pour deux grandes raisons : la première est que le poste de premier ministre n’existait pas dans le gouvernement du BENIN au moment du tournage. La seconde raison est que mon film bien que tourné au BENIN ne parle pas du cas du BENIN mais d’un pays lambda situé en Afrique. N’oublions pas que le film parle également de la corruption internationale et de l’abus des ONG. Les béninois savent bien que le premier ministre actuel est l’architecte du développement du pays. Et soutenir la projection de « UN PAS EN AVANT – Les Dessous de la Corruption » ne ferait que confirmer la bonne volonté du gouvernement dans sa lutte contre la corruption.
Quels sont vos projets ????
Sylvestre Amoussou : Je travaille actuellement sur un autre long métrage qui relate le drame des rapports Nord-Sud. Il faut combattre la corruption pour plus de démocratie en Afrique. Mais pas de manière brutale comme le font les occidentaux. Dénonçons la corruption pour avancer et construire un monde meilleur à nos enfants. Je pense que le cinéma africain a un rôle à jouer. Faire un film coute très cher mais l’Afrique a aussi besoin de rêver. Si elle veut être indépendante elle doit financer son image.
Interview exclusive de Sylvestre Amoussou, accordée le mardi 8 Novembre 2011.
Propos recueillis par Guillaume ADOUVI.
Un pas en avant, les dessous de la corruption.
Film béninois en projection à : l’Espace Saint Michel – 75006 PARIS
Séances : 14 h, 16 h, 18 h, 20 h et 22 h tous les jours.
a4192.en:
That is the title of the latest and second feature film by Sylvestre Amoussou, released this Wednesday 9 November 2011 in France, and showing at the Espace Saint Michel in Paris. ‘Un pas en avant, les dessous de la corruption' (A Step Forward, the Underside of Corruption) is a political thriller in which investigation, twists, suspense, chases and murders follow one another. A thriller that treats, with lightness, a grave universal subject, that of corruption and global humanitarian aid, the latter blithely diverted both downstream and upstream by the actors supposed to administer its management. Sylvestre Amoussou recounts precisely the story of a small craftsman searching for his brother.
And who finally finds himself caught up in a case of embezzlement of humanitarian aid… The main actors — Thierry Desroses, Dieudonné Kabongo, Firmine Richard, Fatou N'Diaye — came from France where they were used to playing secondary roles. The director and the film's production did not skimp on resources, bringing to Benin other secondary actors from Senegal and the West Indies and French technicians. Secondary and extra roles were reserved for local actors. With the exception of Sandra Adjaho, a Beninese actress-performer resident in Benin, who, thanks to a stunning casting, inherited the leading female role, Délali Godomey, the wife of the main character. A role she was able to illuminate with her natural beauty and all her talent as a confirmed actress. Sylvestre Amoussou himself embodies, deploying his immense talent as an actor, with gravity and at times a fine candour, the main character Koffi Godomey; which earned him the prize for best male performance at Fespaco and at the ‘Ecrans noirs' in Cameroon. The film would also win other prizes, such as the prize for best music at Fespaco, etc.
This film, shot in interior sets and in very picturesque African natural settings, aims to be the witness-projector of the image of a radiant Africa, far from the miserabilist clichés of devastating scourges, conflicts and over-mediatised disasters billed by Westerners.
The shooting of the film took place entirely in Benin. The set and the landscapes magnify the cities of Cotonou and Abomey-Calavi, and also sublimate the ecosystems around the lakeside city of Ganvié, with magnificent mangroves, filmed from a new angle never achieved until then, with incredible aerial shots!…
— Sylvestre Amoussou, we are soon going to experience the release of the film ‘Un pas en avant, les dessous de la corruption' in France. What messages do you convey through this work?
Sylvestre Amoussou: Through my film the main message concerns the fight against corruption. Corruption which exists both at the summit of the State and at the level of the ordinary citizen. ‘UN PAS EN AVANT – Les Dessous de la Corruption' cannot by itself change the African situation, but my main intention is to arouse in the viewer the desire to fight against corruption, to take part in local elections, thus taking a step towards democracy. In this film, I also give women back their place. Without women, man is nothing. And I think that with more women in the highest positions there would be less war. A woman always thinks of the future of her children and therefore of the future of her country.
— The Beninese National Assembly adopted on 29 August the bill against corruption and related offences in the Republic of Benin. ‘Un pas en avant, les dessous de la corruption' benefited from assistance from the Beninese government. All this augurs a good will on the part of the Beninese authorities to become aware of the scourge. Are you not planning a collaboration with the government authorities for the distribution of the film in Benin?
Sylvestre Amoussou: I hope this will not be one more law that goes unapplied. I approached the government so that it would organise a screening in BENIN; for the moment that remains a dead letter. I deplore it because I think the government does not give a large enough place to cinema, which can develop a country both humanly and economically. Faced with globalisation, and in the internet era, the government has not grasped the full importance of owning and controlling its image both nationally and internationally. But I do not despair, quite the contrary.
— ‘Les dessous de la corruption', as the title indicates, is a film about corruption. What makes it original?
Sylvestre Amoussou: Its greatest originality: its mode of financing. Indeed, the majority of the funds come both from African civil society and from African politicians who are beginning to understand that only the image they finance can restore a positive image of the continent. Even if the film criticises current African society, it depicts a modern Africa, beautiful and winning. This image will never be financed by the West.
— Making a film requires a lot of financial resources. How did you finance yours, while preserving this originality that is so dear to you?
Sylvestre Amoussou: I was supported by the government of Benin, Beninese civil society, the independent fund of France which contributed 70,000 euros, and the Moroccan cinema centre. The film is totally independent. I am free to say what I see fit. That is very important, because it is neither biased nor slanted. Most African films are financed by France. Which is problematic since in return she wants us to speak about her from her point of view. Moreover, the French media such as France Télévisions refuse to talk about this film because they do not want to give importance to a film that calls into question the relations France maintains with Africa. Few cinemas have agreed to show it. Only the director of the Espace Saint Michel in Paris agreed to show it because he based himself quite simply on the quality of the film. We hope the public will like it so that it will be shown in other cinemas.
— Perfect! So a few institutions and various personalities in Benin and elsewhere in Africa, thus perfectly upright people, but also certainly some corrupted and corrupters, supported you in making this film. Can one see in this a sign of an act of hope thinking of some, and an act of repentance thinking of others among your financiers who themselves have skeletons in the closet in this matter?
Sylvestre Amoussou: In any case I hope so. But it is true that there is a whole education to be redone because the coloniser firmly anchored corruption in our civilisations and some Africans have totally appropriated it and have even become masters of it. Our dialects do not possess the word ‘corruption'. The French language does! And let us not forget that for there to be corrupted people there must at the base be corrupters.
— We saw that certain members of the government of the country in which the film is set were ‘hyper-corrupt', notably the Prime Minister. Do you not fear a possible confusion with the members of the Beninese government given that the film was entirely shot in Benin?
Sylvestre Amoussou: No. The film was indeed entirely shot in Benin, it is simply a choice to showcase our country, through these beautiful landscapes and its infrastructural effort to meet international tourism standards. The country in which the film is set remains the United States of Africa. You can see moreover that its flag is a star-spangled banner representing all the African states. Nor is there any possible confusion between the current prime minister of BENIN and the corrupt prime minister of my film. For two main reasons: the first is that the post of prime minister did not exist in the government of BENIN at the time of shooting. The second reason is that my film, although shot in BENIN, does not speak of the case of BENIN but of a generic country situated in Africa. Let us not forget that the film also speaks of international corruption and of the abuse of NGOs. Beninese people know well that the current prime minister is the architect of the country's development. And supporting the screening of ‘UN PAS EN AVANT – Les Dessous de la Corruption' would only confirm the government's good will in its fight against corruption.
— What are your projects????
Sylvestre Amoussou: I am currently working on another feature film which recounts the drama of North-South relations. Corruption must be fought for more democracy in Africa. But not in a brutal way as Westerners do. Let us denounce corruption in order to move forward and build a better world for our children. I think African cinema has a role to play. Making a film costs a great deal but Africa also needs to dream. If she wants to be independent she must finance her own image.
Exclusive interview with Sylvestre Amoussou, granted on Tuesday 8 November 2011.
Interview conducted by Guillaume ADOUVI.
Un pas en avant, les dessous de la corruption.
Beninese film screening at: l'Espace Saint Michel – 75006 PARIS
Showings: 2 p.m., 4 p.m., 6 p.m., 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. every day.

a4364.t:
(ክፍል አንድ)
በአመሐ ኃይለ ማርያም
ከአፄ ኃይለ ሥላሴ እስከ መንግሥቱ ኃይለ ማርያም፣ ከመለስ ዜናዊ እስከ ዓብይ አህመድ (ዶ/ር) የዘመናዊዋ ኢትዮጵያ መሪዎች ማንነት፣ ዕሳቤ፣ ሕልምና ምኞት በኢኮኖሚ አመራራቸው ውስጥ በእጅጉ ይንፀባረቃል፡፡ ከጽሑፌ መደምደሚያ ለመጀመር፣ የጠቅላይ ሚኒስትር ዓብይ (ዶ/ር) የኢኮኖሚ አመራር ብዙ ተስፋ፣ ትንሽ ተግባራትና ትልልቅ ሥጋቶች የተስተዋሉበትና የሚያንዣብቡበት ነው። ነገርን ከሥሩ ውኃን ከጥሩ እንዲሉ አበው ትንሽ ወደኋላ ለመመለስ ያህል 43 ዓመታትን በሥልጣን ያሳለፉትና በተማሪዎች እንቢተኝነት ከዙፋናቸው የተነሱት ንጉሡ፣ ፊውዳላዊ በሆነ መዋቅር ያስተዳደሩት የነበረው ኢኮኖሚ ጥገኝነቱ በግብርና ላይ ሆኖ ተቋማዊ ኢኮኖሚስቶች (Institutional Economists) እንደሚሉት ‹‹በዝባዥ›› የነበረ ሥርዓት ነበር፡፡ መገለጫውም የምርት ሒደት ሰንሰለቶች፣ እንዲሁም የመሠረታዊ ምርት ግብዓቶች የበላይ ጠባቂነት በባላባቱ ክፍል ተይዞ አብዛኛው አምራች ኃይል በገባርነት የሚተዳደርበት፣ ምሪቱ ካፒታሊስታዊ ሆኖ ሥሪቱ ግን ወደ ባለባት ያጋደለ የኢኮኖሚ ሥርዓት ነበር፡፡
የዚህ ሥርዓት ካፒታሊስታዊ መግለጫዎች የሆኑት የገበያ ተኮር ተቋማት ሥርጭት ግን የባላባቱ ክፍል በሚኖርባቸው አካባቢዎች የተገደበና እጅግ በጣም ውስንነት የሚስተዋልበት ነበር፡፡ ሥርዓቱ ከጊዜ ወደ ጊዜ እየተስፋፋ የመጣውን የባላባት ክፍል ፍላጎት ለማሟላት በሚያስችል መልኩ የተደራጀ ቢሆንም የጤና፣ የትምህርት፣ የመሠረተ ልማትና የገበያ ተቋማት ግንባታም ይካሄድ ነበር፡፡ ለዚህም ምሳሌ የሚሆኑት አሁን ድረስ ያሉት መንግሥታዊና ለትርፍ የተቋቋሙ የመንግሥት ድርጅቶች ለምሳሌ የኢትዮጵያ አየር መንገድ፣ የንግድ መርከብ ድርጅት፣ የኢትዮጵያ ንግድ ባንክ፣ ወዘተ የተመሠረቱት በዚያን ጊዜ ነው፡፡ በአርባ ሦስቱ የንጉሡ አገዛዝ ዓመታት የጠቅላላ አገራዊ ምርት ዕድገት በዝቅተኛ ደረጃ ያድግ የነበረ ሲሆን፣ አማካይ ዕድገቱም ከሁለት እስከ አምስት በመቶ ይሆን ነበር፡፡ የመንግሥት በጀት ወደ ካፒታል በጀት ያጋድል የነበረ ሲሆን፣ ጠንካራ ምንዛሪ ያለው መገበያያ (Currency) የዘመኑ መገለጫ ነበር፡፡ የወቅቱ የበጀት ጉድለት በዝቅተኛ ደረጃ መቆየቱ አጠቃላይ ኢኮኖሚያዊ መረጋጋትን ቢያመለክትም የካፒታል እጥረት ግን ኢኮኖሚውን የሚገዳደርበት ጊዜ ነበር፡፡
የመንግሥት ወጪ የተገደበ (Restrained) ሆኖ ለረጅም ጊዜ የቆየ ሲሆን፣ በአንፃራዊነት የተሻለ የምንጭ ልዩነት የሚስተዋልበት የመንግሥት ገቢ ሥርዓት ነበር፡፡ የንጉሡ አስተዳደር በዕርዳታ ፍለጋና በውጭ ግንኙነት ረገድ ጠንካራ የሚባል አቅም ነበረው፡፡ ለዚህም ይመስላል ትልልቅ የሚባሉ የበረሃማነት መከላከል፣ የተፋሰስ ልማት፣ የተፈጥሮ ሀብት ፍለጋዎችና ልማት፣ የውኃ ኃይል ማመንጫዎች፣ የምርት ማቀነባበሪያዎች፣ የምርት ማጓጓዝ አደረጃጀትና የመሳሰሉት ኢኮኖሚያዊ እንቅስቃሴዎችን በለጋሾች ድጋፍ ማጥናት፣ ማስጀመርና መተግበር የተቻለው፡፡ ብዙዎቹ ዛሬ ላይ ‹‹አገራዊ›› ተብለው ትልቅ ፖለቲካዊ ዋጋ የሚሰጣቸው ፕሮጀክቶች የተጠነሰሱት፣ የተጠኑትና የዲዛይን ሥራ የተሠራላቸው በዚያ ወቅት መሆኑን ልብ ይሏል፡፡ ለዚህም የህዳሴው ግድብና በሶማሌ ክልል የሚገኘው የተፈጥሮ ጋዝ ፍለጋና ልማት ፕሮጀክቶች ማሳያ ናቸው፡፡
የኋላ ኋላ ግን በዝባዥ የነበረው የንጉሡ ኢኮኖሚያዊ አስተዳደር መዋቅር በአንድ በኩል የኢኮኖሚ ጫናው በመረረው አምራች ሕዝብ፣ በሌላ በኩል እየተቀየረ በመጣው ዓለም አቀፋዊ ኢኮኖሚያዊ ሥሪት ውስጥ እያደገ የመጣው የገቢ ዋጋ ንረት (በዋናነት የነዳጅ ምርቶች ዋጋ) ባመጣው ወቅታዊ ኢኮኖሚያዊ አለመመጣጠንና ያን ተከትሎ በገነፈለው ሕዝባዊ እንቢተኝነት ተንገዳግዶች ለመውደቅ በቅቷል፡፡ አንባቢያን እዚህ ላይ ሊይዝ የሚገባው የመዋቅራዊ አለመመጣጠኑ ውጤት ዕለታዊ ገጽታዎች ለተራዘሙ ዘመናት የኢኮኖሚ ተጠቃሚነት ጥያቄን በኅብረተሰቡ ውስጥ ሲያስነሱ መኖራቸውን፣ ይህም በተዛባው ምሪትም ቢሆን (ጥቂት የገዥ መደብ አገልጋይ ባለሙያዎችን መፍጠርን ዓላማው ያደረገ) በተፈጠሩት የተማሪና የሙያተኛ ክፍሎች ለተራዘሙ ዘመናት ይስተዋል የነበረ መሆኑን ነው፡፡ በተጋጋለው የተማሪዎች፣ የባለሙያዎችና በጠቅላላ ሕዝባዊ አመፅ ንጉሡ ከሥልጣን ቢወገዱም እንዳሰቡት መግባባት ያልቻሉት ተማሪዎች በሀልዮታዊ የትርጉም ልዩነት ጎራ ይዘው ሲፈሳፈሱ ሥልጣን መያዝ አልቻሉም። ይልቁንም የእነሱን ፍስፍስ እንደ ድክመትና ጥሩ አጋጣሚ ያየው የታጠቀ ኃይል ራሱን ወደ ሥልጣን አስጠግቶ ለዘመኑ ስሜት በመረጠው ሃሳዊ ሶሻሊስታዊ (Pseudo-Socialist) አስተዳደር ኢትዮጵያን ለ17 ዓመታት ማስተዳደር ቻለ፡፡ በኮሎኔል መንግሥቱ ኃይለ ማርያም የሚመራው የደርግ መንግሥት በኢኮኖሚ አስተዳደር ረገድ ከንጉሡ አስተዳደር የተለየ ነበር፡፡ የአስተዳደሩ ሥሪት የሀብት ክፍፍል ሚዛናዊነት (Distributive Fairness) ለማምጣት የሚተጋ፣ መሠረታዊ የምርት ግብዓቶች ባለቤትነትንም ለሰፊው ሕዝብ የመለሰ ነበር፡፡ የአስተዳደሩ የመጀመሪያ ዕርምጃ እንዲያውም መሬትን ለአራሹ ኅብረተሰብ ክፍል በመመለስ የፊውዳላዊ ምርት ሥርዓትን መሠረት መናድ ነበር፡፡ በዚህም ከፍተኛ ሕዝባዊ ተቀባይነት (ለጊዜውም ቢሆን) ማግኘት ችሏል፡፡
የደርግ መንግሥት ኢኮኖሚያዊ አስተዳደር እንደ ንጉሡ ሁሉ በጠቋሚና መካከለኛ ዘመን ዕቅዶች የሚመራ ሲሆን ትኩረቱ አንፃራዊ እኩልነት የሚስተዋልበት ኅብረተሰብ መገንባት የሚል ነበር፡፡ ችግሩ ይህ አንፃራዊ እኩልነትን መፍጠር የሚለው ሶሻሊስታዊ አጀንዳ ግለሰባዊ ኢኮኖሚያዊ ማበረታቻዎችን (Economic Incentive) ማዳከሙና ይህም ምርታማነትን በመገደብ ሀብት ፈጠራን ማኮስመኑ ነው፡፡ ባልተፈጠረ ሀብት ላይ የተጫነው ሀብትን የማከፋፈል መዋቅራዊ ሥሌት ኅብረተሰቡን በጋራ ወደ ባለፀግነት ከመምራት ይልቅ ወደ ጋራ ድህነት እንዲያሽቆለቁል አደረገው፡፡ ምንም እንኳን የምርት አላባዎች ባለቤትነትን ቢረጋገጥም የግብዓት እጥረት ጠፍንጎ ይዞት የግብርና ምርታማነት ከዳዴ የተሻለ ጉዞ ማድረግ አልቻለም፡፡ እንዲያውም ከ17 ዓመታት ውስጥ ግማሽ ያህሉን በእንፉቅቅ ነው ሲሄድ የነበረው፡፡ በውስጣዊ የእርስ በርስ ግጭትና ጦርነት እንዲሁም በውጭ ኃይሎች የድንበር ይገባኛል ጥያቄ አጣብቂኝ ውስጥ የገባው ደርግ፣ ከገቢው ወጪው በመብዛቱ ዕድሜውን የገፋው ‹‹በሶሻሊስታዊ ወንድማማችነት›› በሚሰጡት ብድሮችና ድጎማዎች ነበር፡፡ በእንቅርት ላይ ጆሮ ደግፍ እንዲሉ፣ ላይነቃነቅ የተቸከለው የመገበያያ ገንዘብ ፖሊሲ ትክክለኛ የምንዛሪ ሥርዓትን አለመከተሉ ሳያንስ ችካሉን ለማስጠበቅ የሚወጣው ድጎማ በእጅጉ ብዙ ነበር፡፡ በጥቅሉ የደርግ ሥርዓት ኢኮኖሚ ከጅምሩ ለውድቀት የተፈጠረ (Destined to Fail) መሆኑን አረጋግጧል፡፡ ይህም ሆኖ ሥርዓቱ ትምህርትን፣ ጤናንና እንዲሁም የግብርና ቴክኖሎጂን በማቅረብ ረገድ ከፍ ያለ እመርታን ማስመዝገብ መቻሉ ተመዝግቧል፡፡

ምንም እንኳን ይህ ጉዳይ በገዥው ፓርቲ ውስጥ እንደ አጀንዳ ከቀረበ ቢቆይም ባለመግባባቶች ቆይቶ ውሳኔ የተሰጠበት የዓብይ አስተዳደር ወደ ሥልጣን በወጣ በጥቂት ሳምንታት ውስጥ ነበር፡፡ ይህን ውሳኔ ግዙፍ የሚያደርገው ኢሕአዴግ መራሹ መንግሥት ለብዙ ዓመታት እንደማይነኩ ጫፎች ሲቆጥራቸው የነበሩት፣ ገቢ በማስገኘት ረገድም ቁልፍ ሚና የነበራቸው የመንግሥት የንግድ ተቋማት የተካተቱበት በመሆኑ ነው። ውሳኔው የኢትዮ ቴሌኮም፣ የኢትዮጵያ ባህር ትራንስፖርትና ሎጂስቲክስ አገልግሎት ድርጅት፣ የኢትዮጵያ አየር መንገድና የምድር ባቡር ኮርፖሬሽን በውስጡ ማቀፉ ነው፡፡ ከዚህ በመለስ ይህ ውሳኔ የስኳር ፋብሪካዎችን፣ የማዳበሪያ ፋብሪካዎችንና ሌሎች ድርጅቶችን ያካተተ ነበር፡፡ በእርግጥም ውሳኔውና ለውሳኔው መነሻ ሆነዋል የተባሉት ችግሮች አለመጣጣም ይታይባቸዋል፡፡ እንደ መንግሥት ገለጻ ይህ ውሳኔ አካታች፣ ቀጣይነት ያለውና የዘመነ ኢኮኖሚ ለመፍጠር በሚል የተወሰነ ነው፡፡ በሌላው ወገን መንግሥት ራሱ ደግሞ ውሳኔው የብድር ጫናን ለማቅለል፣ የውጭ ምንዛሪን ለማግኘት፣ አገልግሎት አሰጣጥን ለማሻሻልና መንግሥታዊ ወጪን ለመቀነስ የተወሰደ ዕርምጃ ነው ይላል፡፡ በሁለቱም ወገን የሚነሱት ምክንያቶች እውነተኛ ቢሆኑ እንኳን የመድረሻና የመንገድ አለመጣጣም ይስተዋልባቸዋል፡፡ መዋቅራዊ ችግር ጠፍንጎት ዝቅተኛ የግብርና ምርታማነት፣ የተንሰራፋ የገበያ ዝንፈትና ረዥም የገበያ ሰንሰለት፣ ያልተደራጀ የገበያ ቁጥጥርና አቅም፣ በመንግሥት ጥገኝነት የተፈጠረና ተወዳዳሪነትን የሚፈራ የግል ዘርፍ፣ እየሰፋ የመጣ የወጪ ንግድና ክፍያ ሚዛን፣ የተንሸዋረረ የጉልበት ገበያና ሌሎች አያሌ ችግሮች ለሚዘውሩት ኢኮኖሚ ሁነኛ መላው የመንግሥት (የሕዝብ) ተቋማትን ወደ ግል ማዛወር ነው የሚለው መከራከሪያ ግራ የሚያጋባ ነው፡፡ በዚያ ላይ ይህ ሁሉ የሚሆነው ግልጽ የሆነ የሽያጭ ሥርዓት ባልተደራጀበት፣ የአክሲዮን ገበያ መሠረተ ልማት በሌለበት፣ የመንግሥት ተቋማት የመቆጣጠር አቅም ባልጠነከረበት፣ ፖለቲካዊ ምኅዳሩ በጥገኛ ባለሀብቱ ሥር በወደቀበት ሁኔታ መሆኑን ነገሩን የበለጠ ግራ ያደርገዋል፡፡ ለነገሩ ተባለ እንጂ አፈጻጸሙ ዓመታትን መውሰዱ ዕሙን ነው፡፡ (ክፍል ሁለት ሳምንት ይቀጥላል)
ከአዘጋጁ፡- ጸሐፊው በሰሜን አሜሪካ የሚኖሩ የፋይናንስ ዘርፍ ባለሙያ ሲሆኑ፣ ጽሑፉ የእሳቸውን አመለካከት ብቻ የሚያንፀባርቅ መሆኑን እንገልጻለን፡፡

(Part One)
By Ameha Haile Mariam

From Emperor Haile Selassie to Mengistu Haile Mariam, from Meles Zenawi to Abiy Ahmed (PhD), the identity, thinking, dreams and ambitions of modern Ethiopia’s leaders are strongly reflected in their economic leadership. To begin from my conclusion: Prime Minister Abiy’s (PhD) economic leadership is one in which much hope, few accomplishments and great risks have been observed and continue to loom. To go back a little — as the elders say, take a matter from its root and water from its source — the Emperor, who spent 43 years in power and was removed from his throne by student defiance, presided over an economy managed through a feudal structure, dependent on agriculture and, as institutional economists would call it, an “exploitative” system. Its hallmark was that the production chains and the guardianship of basic inputs of production were held by the nobility while most of the productive force lived as tribute-payers; the orientation was capitalist but the make-up leaned toward the aristocracy.

The distribution of the market-oriented institutions that were the capitalist expressions of this system was, however, confined to the areas where the nobility lived and was extremely limited. Although the system was organized so as to meet the ever-expanding demands of the aristocratic class, construction of health, education, infrastructure and market institutions also took place. Examples are the state and for-profit government enterprises that still exist today — Ethiopian Airlines, the Shipping Lines, the Commercial Bank of Ethiopia and so on — all of which were founded in that period. Over the 43 years of the Emperor’s rule, gross domestic product grew at a low level, averaging between two and five percent. The government budget leaned toward capital expenditure, and a currency with a hard exchange value was a hallmark of the era. Although the low budget deficit of the time indicated general economic stability, capital shortage was a constant challenge to the economy.

Government spending remained restrained for a long time, and the government revenue system showed a relatively good diversity of sources. The Emperor’s administration had strong capacity in seeking aid and in foreign relations. That is probably why it was possible, with donor support, to study, launch and implement major economic activities such as desertification control, watershed development, natural resource exploration and development, hydropower plants, processing plants, transport organization and the like. Note that many of the projects that today are called “national” and given great political value were conceived, studied and designed in that period. The Renaissance Dam and the natural gas exploration and development projects in the Somali Regional State are illustrations.

Eventually, however, the Emperor’s exploitative economic administrative structure was shaken and fell — on one side because of the producing population embittered by economic pressure, and on the other because of the economic imbalance of the moment brought about by rising import prices (mainly petroleum products) within a changing global economic order, and the popular defiance that erupted in its wake. What readers should grasp here is that the daily manifestations of that structural imbalance had for extended periods raised questions of economic benefit within society, and that this was visible for long periods among the student and professional classes created even by the distorted educational orientation (whose aim was to produce a few professionals serving the ruling class). Although the Emperor was removed from power by the intensified revolt of students, professionals and the public at large, the students, who could not agree as they had hoped, splintered into camps over doctrinal differences of interpretation and were unable to take power. Rather, the armed force, which saw their fragmentation as weakness and a good opportunity, brought itself to power and managed to rule Ethiopia for 17 years under a pseudo-socialist administration chosen to suit the mood of the era. The Derg government led by Colonel Mengistu Haile Mariam was different from the Emperor’s administration in economic management. Its make-up strove to bring distributive fairness and returned ownership of the basic means of production to the broad public. Its first step was indeed to return land to the tiller, dismantling the foundation of the feudal production system. With this it gained great popular acceptance (even if only temporarily).

The Derg government’s economic administration, like the Emperor’s, was guided by indicative and medium-term plans, and its focus was building a society in which relative equality would be visible. The problem is that this socialist agenda of creating relative equality weakened individual economic incentives, which in turn limited productivity and stunted wealth creation. A structural calculus of distributing wealth imposed upon wealth that had not been created drove society down toward shared poverty rather than leading it to shared prosperity. Although ownership of the factors of production was secured, input shortages held it in a grip and agricultural productivity could not advance beyond a crawl. Indeed, about half of the 17 years were spent limping. Caught in internal civil conflict and war as well as in border claims by external forces, the Derg, whose expenditure exceeded its revenue, prolonged its life on the loans and subsidies given in “socialist brotherhood.” To make matters worse, on top of an immovably pegged currency policy that failed to follow a correct exchange-rate regime, the subsidy spent to defend the peg was enormous. On the whole, the Derg system’s economy proved to have been destined to fail. Even so, it is on record that the system registered great advances in delivering education, health and agricultural technology.

It was at the time when the Western capitalist world had confirmed its global supremacy and when the Eastern socialist ideology had been defeated in its doctrinal existence after the collapse of the Soviet Union that the EPRDF, which defeated the Derg system in a protracted armed struggle, came to power. To reconcile the ideological conflict it faced when a socialist force that had spent 17 years in armed struggle came to power, and to bring itself into accord with international reality, it made free-market economic management its guiding system even though it did not believe in it. It testified at the time that the system the country was following was “white capitalism.” The mixed-economy principle the Derg applied in its final days of distress was stretched and put to work in the EPRDF era. The EPRDF announced that it wanted to create a system in which the comparison of demand and supply guides the market, in which basic economic inputs are managed under individual ownership, in which ownership of wealth is permitted without limit, in which market chains operate without quotas and without pressure, in which market institutions organize freely, and in which wealth creation receives economic incentive. Following this, the currency was taken off a fixed exchange rate and made to be determined, in a measured way, through competition among banks. Building the country’s economy after a protracted war was, however, no easy task. Using the country’s politics and their own international weight, Western countries did not fail to exert pressure on Ethiopia to follow their political-economy model.

In this respect the role of the World Bank and the IMF was extremely prominent. The option these institutions offered our country — gripped by a shortage of finance and still struggling to emerge from the ruin of war — was that if she wanted their financial support she must open her banking, telecom and transport sectors to competition and make the monetary and foreign-trade system market-led (liberalized). The main agenda behind their conception, however, was to provide indirect policy support so that the big companies of the Western world would control the country’s key economic sectors early on. The renowned economist and Nobel Prize laureate Joseph Stiglitz, in his book “Globalization and Its Discontents,” describes how Ethiopia’s policymakers of the time (primarily Meles Zenawi) struggled hard to withstand this policy pressure, and how, in the end, standing firm in refusal, they lost the temporary recovery financing they were to have received. Stiglitz calls this struggle a struggle to create independent policy-making capacity, and says it rescued Ethiopia from the Structural Adjustment Program that these institutions were spreading internationally at the time and from the process whose damage has still not disappeared in various economies.

Just as the withered economy was reviving, the central government was consolidating its power, the former fighters who are now the leaders were learning to govern, and relative peace was spreading, the border conflict with Eritrea broke out. For an Ethiopian economy that had not yet shed the smell of gunpowder, that was straining to stand on its two feet, and that was also wrestling with external pressure, the war was a severe test. For Meles Zenawi’s government, which had drawn up a reconstruction strategy and was moving to bring change in infrastructure, reconstruction, the delivery of basic services, peace and stability, incremental agricultural improvement, and improvements in education and health provision, the fire ignited against it by its former comrades-in-arms was a great trial. On one side, because it was not prepared for the invasion, it faced an organizational test in manpower and weapons capacity. Gathering back the demobilized army it had dispersed in order to come out of the war victorious, persuading trained soldiers and officers who had been in the former army, recruiting and training willing conscripts — these were tasks demanding very high immediate expenditure. On the other side, in addition to the weapons it had accumulated during the protracted struggle (mostly captured from the Derg army), it was necessary to buy new armaments. Given the economic reality of the time, this seemed altogether impossible. Although, with Western assistance and with a rapid and all-inclusive societal response, the war was concluded at the cost of tens of thousands of lives, its scar has nevertheless remained a negative legacy for both countries’ economies.

The consequences of the Ethio-Eritrean war also spilled over to the ruling party. The comrades of the bush, who did not agree on the conduct and execution strategy of the war, brought the differences among them into the open, and the TPLF, said to be the core of the ruling party, faced the danger of splitting. In economic leadership, this internal difference and the TPLF split that followed had a positive role. It created an opportunity that underlined that more was expected of an administration that previously had no dream beyond reconstruction, and that this could be secured only by changing the all-round condition of citizens. That is why all the analysts who praise Ethiopia’s economic growth and Meles Zenawi’s greatness start their economic calendar from this period. Having won the internal division through a Bonapartist analysis, Meles Zenawi, after distancing his rivals from the scene by various tactics, focused his main attention on contemplating, writing and implementing the economic design of his choice. As the organization’s political doctrine had earlier been named “revolutionary democracy,” Meles affirmed that very doctrine and made “developmental state” its instrument of implementation.

The developmental state, which in many of its features is the opposite of the liberal-state concept, makes economic structural transformation its main focus and takes human-capital building, the building of institutions capable of curbing rent-seeking, prudence in budget use, and tight monetary policy as its main principles. This economic principle, which holds that the economy “must not be left to the market and to marketeers alone; rather the state should be an active participant in it,” deeply detests watching the economy from the sidelines. By contrast, it believes the state should have an active role in selecting and supporting those actors who, beyond filling market gaps, will have a greater role in ensuring sustainable development. For this purpose it holds that the state may have a role extending even to deliberately creating market distortions. Both Meles and Hailemariam led Ethiopia by this economic principle, copied from East Asian countries and whose actual existence stands in opposition to the liberal state. Although its ideal existence was to ensure development by saving capital and to improve citizens’ lives, the outcomes the developmental state produced in Ethiopia were mixed.

On one hand the principle enabled rapid growth of gross domestic product (GDP), better access to infrastructure, improvement in the delivery of social services, and the attraction of higher foreign investment. On the other hand it is plagued by heavy poverty pressure combined with rapid population growth, rising unemployment, exports that could not improve, a heavy debt burden, and growing wealth inequality. In a sense, one can say the developmental state is its own enemy. Why? Because while it struggles along with an economy that could not create enough jobs, on the other side, through the higher-education institutions it builds (it would be easier to say “grows”) with the wealth it pours in, it also produces thousands of half-baked graduates. Even leaving aside the yearly decline in the quality of education and of the graduates, which seems unreconciled with reality, the failure to work so that the number of graduates matches the capacity to employ is a fact that betrays that the developmental state was tying its own feet. In a country where more than 70 percent of the population is under 35 and where the poverty rate reaches about 38 percent, although coordinated economic leadership ought to come from the state structure, the other face of the developmental state is worsening waste of resources and corruption. The state development enterprises that wore developmental intervention and strategic protection like a hat, on one side accommodated great waste of resources and, on the other, threw their doors wide open to overnight enrichment for their managers.

Matters worsened after Ato Meles Zenawi, the originator and chief guardian of the developmental state idea, died and Ato Hailemariam Desalegn, whose political capital was extremely thin, replaced him in his post. Ato Meles’s death greatly emboldened “state thieves” and, by creating a leadership vacuum, was an event that sent the waste of resources sky-high all at once. What must be borne in mind here is that about 85 percent of the total economy’s consumption is governmental, expressed through services, projects, fixed assets and consumable purchases. Hence, if the method of creating overnight rich men is corruption, it cannot be realized without their governmental partners. And that is exactly what happened. As if the spread of the waste of resources and corruption were not enough, the fact that the poor paid the price through the inflation created by this ill-gotten wealth was an injury on top of an injury. Even the subsidy activities carried out to support the livelihood of the poor became sites of great waste, entrenched chains of patronage and limitless corruption. Ato Hailemariam’s emaciated political capital made control impossible and greed knew no bounds.

The popular defiance that began in opposition to the plan called “the Integrated Master Plan of Addis Ababa and its Surroundings” broadened its focus and began to shake the country, carrying demands for all-round freedom, equitable economic benefit, the prevalence of justice and fairness, accountability, practical self-administration, governmental transparency and the like. The EPRDF-led government, whose answer to such protest had customarily been force, was caught in a bind — on one side by the breadth of the protest, on the other by pressure from its own members who openly and covertly stood with the protesters. Change, however, could not come easily. After three years of popular defiance, many deaths and maimings, thousands of arrests, much waste and destruction of property, widespread economic slowdown, two states of emergency, much social crisis (displacement, migration and instability), as well as much intercession and external pressure, the EPRDF turned to look at itself. The resignation of the front’s chairman and Prime Minister Hailemariam Desalegn opened the door for a new leadership to come. The EPRDF, after a 17-day extended evaluation, found its new chairman, Abiy Ahmed. And a glimmer of hope shone in the hearts of citizens. Seven years and six months have been counted since Abiy Ahmed’s (PhD) administration came to power, and it has taken numerous steps by which it may be evaluated. Leaving its political steps aside for now, let us focus on its economic steps. The administration’s biggest and principal step is the one it took regarding for-profit state development enterprises. In this, on one side it decided to sell some development enterprises entirely to private investors, and on the other it decided to transfer a certain share of some others to private investors.

Although this matter had been on the agenda within the ruling party for some time, it was decided — after disagreements — within a few weeks of the Abiy administration’s coming to power. What makes this decision momentous is that it included the state commercial institutions that the EPRDF-led government had for many years counted as untouchable summits and that had a key role in generating revenue. The decision encompassed Ethio Telecom, the Ethiopian Shipping and Logistics Services Enterprise, Ethiopian Airlines and the Railway Corporation. Beyond these, the decision included sugar factories, fertilizer factories and other enterprises. Indeed, an inconsistency is visible between the decision and the problems said to have prompted it. According to the government, this decision was taken in order to create an inclusive, sustainable and modernized economy. On the other hand, the government itself says the decision was a step taken to ease the debt burden, to obtain foreign exchange, to improve service delivery and to reduce government expenditure. Even if the reasons raised on both sides were true, an inconsistency between destination and road is observable. The argument that the sure remedy for an economy driven by low agricultural productivity gripped by structural problems, widespread market distortion and long market chains, disorganized market regulation and capacity, a private sector created in dependence on the state and afraid of competition, a widening trade and payments balance, a skewed labour market and many other problems is to transfer state (public) institutions into private hands is confusing. On top of that, the fact that all this is happening where no transparent sales system has been organized, where there is no stock-market infrastructure, where the regulatory capacity of state institutions has not strengthened, and where the political space has fallen under dependent capitalists, makes the matter even more confusing. In any case, it was only said — its execution has certainly taken years. (Part two continues next week.)

From the editor: The writer is a finance-sector professional living in North America, and we note that the article reflects only his own views.

                                By  Eden Sahle  
                                
                            
For decades, African countries, including Ethiopia, have heavily relied on financial aid and humanitarian assistance from developed nations, particularly the United States and European states.
America’s recent decision to withdraw support from key international organisations, including the World Health Organization (WHO) and major aid programs, has triggered a crisis affecting healthcare, food security, and economic stability across the continent.
The United States has historically been one of Africa’s largest aid providers. According to the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), in 2021 alone, America provided approximately 8.5 billion dollars in aid to sub-Saharan Africa, funding healthcare, economic development, humanitarian assistance, and security programs.
While aid has not completely dried up, European nations, particularly the European Union (EU), the United Kingdom, and France, continue to provide substantial support. The EU contributes around 25 billion euro annually in development aid, making it Africa’s largest donor.
However, the US remains the single largest donor to health initiatives in Africa. The President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) has provided over 100 billion dollars since 2003 to combat HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria across the continent, including Ethiopia. The Feed the Future programme has supported millions of African farmers and families, while the US has led emergency relief efforts in famine-stricken and conflict-ridden regions such as Sudan, Ethiopia, and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
The US withdrawal is already taking a toll on funding for critical organisations like WHO, UNICEF, and the World Food Programme (WFP). The consequences are a reduction in vaccine distribution and disease control programs, decline in emergency food assistance for millions facing hunger, and a slowdown in economic aid, impacting infrastructure projects and employment opportunities.
According to the WHO, more than 1.5 million African children receive life-saving vaccines annually through US-funded programmes. With this support in jeopardy, there might be potential outbreaks of diseases like measles and polio, which had been largely under control.
Africa’s healthcare system remains heavily dependent on foreign donors. The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, & Malaria (GFATM) reports that over 70pc of Africa’s HIV/AIDS programmes rely on international funding. A cut in aid could mean reduced access to antiretroviral drugs for 25 million people living with HIV across the continent.
America's withdrawal from key food aid programs also threatens millions, worsening malnutrition across Africa. Despite years of assistance, the continent remains one of the most food-insecure regions in the world. The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) estimates that 278 million people in Africa face chronic hunger.
Ethiopia is particularly vulnerable to these aid cuts. Data suggests that America’s withdrawal could put Ethiopia under greater strain than most African countries.
The United States has historically been Ethiopia’s largest bilateral donor, providing financial and humanitarian assistance for healthcare, education, economic development, and security. According to USAID, Ethiopia received approximately 1.8 billion dollars in 2022 alone, making it one of the largest recipients of American aid in Africa.
The US has been a major funder of Ethiopia’s healthcare system, particularly through PEPFAR, which has helped provide antiretroviral treatment to over half a million Ethiopians living with HIV. America has also provided emergency aid in response to droughts, locust infestations, and conflicts, benefiting over 20 million people in need of urgent assistance.
Ethiopia’s healthcare system remains heavily dependent on external funding. The Global Fund reports that over 60pc of the country’s HIV/AIDS programs rely on foreign aid. Meanwhile, the Ethiopian Ministry of Health (MoH) estimates that the country needs at least 2 billion dollars annually to sustain essential health services.
Beyond the immediate crisis, the decline in foreign aid presents an opportunity for African governments to take responsibility for their citizens and build sustainable, self-reliant economies.
While foreign aid has addressed critical issues, it has also fostered dependency. The reduction of US aid should be a turning point for African leaders to prioritise self-sufficiency and invest in their people's welfare.
African states must allocate more resources to healthcare. The 2001 Abuja Declaration recommended that at least 15pc of government spending go to healthcare, yet many countries fall short, relying on aid to fill the gap.
Instead of depending on foreign donors, Africa should expand local vaccine manufacturing. Rwanda, South Africa, and Egypt have already begun developing domestic production facilities, proving it can be done. Scaling up these efforts across the continent is now more critical than ever.
Africa imports 50 billion dollars worth of food annually. Countries like Ghana and Kenya have successfully reduced reliance on food imports by supporting local farmers through subsidies and market access.
Investment in manufacturing, technology, and industrialisation will create jobs and reduce dependence on aid.
Transparency and accountability are essential. According to the African Union, corruption costs Africa 148 billion dollars annually, money that could be used for healthcare, education, and infrastructure.
The African diaspora contributes over 50 billion dollars annually in remittances. Encouraging investment from Africans abroad could finance development projects and further reduce reliance on foreign aid.
By increasing domestic investment in healthcare, agriculture, and economic diversification, Africa can take control of its future. The time for leaders to act is now.

a4420.t:
Civil servants and armed forces in South Sudan have received salary arrears for February and March 2025, Vice President for Economic Cluster Dr. Benjamin Bol Mel said, in what he describes as the government’s commitment to improving public service delivery.
In a statement on 24th March, Vice President Bol said he has fulfilled his previous pledge to expedite the prompt payment of civil servant salaries on the 24th of every month.
He further revealed that a roadmap for the progressive clearance of all outstanding salary arrears will be unveiled.
Dr. Bol also said the Bank of South Sudan has now established what he referred to as “ring fenced” public salary account dedicated to salary disbursement.
The government has been struggling to meet its expenditures and civil servants and armed forces were not paid for one year after the main pipeline pumping oil from South Sudan through Sudan for export was damaged in February 2024 during the Sudan war.
The pipeline has since been repaired and the government announced the resumption of crude export.
Meanwhile, some government officials and civil servants in Eastern Equatoria have expressed mixed reaction after the state employees received one month’s salary in the Torit.
Speaking to a state-owned radio, Minister of Finance Peter Lokuju Lotirmoi, confirmed the payments and urged public to be patient while waiting for the other accumulated arrears.
“It is true that the vice president fulfilled whatever he promised. So, our people today, they are receiving their salaries. Everybody now is okay, because our vice president is serious in whatever he promised,” Lotirmoi said.
“I want the people to be patient. Again, I want the people to be ready to receive the March salaries. Let them be patient for some five or four days. We are going to release the other ones also. They are already with us.”
SPLM-IO Member of Parliament Kokol Michael appealed to Vice President Bol to promptly pay the pending months of civil servants’ salaries. He also called for economic reform to ensure the restoration of the value of South Sudan pounds.
“I welcome and appreciate that one man given. We hope that the Vice President of Economic Cluster has to continue meeting what he has promised to the civil servant.”
“What we are currently receiving is an arrears, not the salaries because the salaries are paid immediately at end of the month.”
“The Vice President of Economic cluster has to strengthen the issue of economy so that specifically the rate of dollars and pounds can stabilize, dollars have become stronger and the pounds which civil servants are receiving is completely very low when we go to the market.”
For her part, Ajok Grace, a civil servant, expressed frustrations over delayed salary payment since 2024 which she said has made life difficult for citizens across the state.
“Looking at the current situation of the citizens, we all know it has not been fine with us because people have been trying like struggling here and there,” he said.
“Though the salary was not there, the sacrifice was being given to the services of the nation. But at the end of the day, you find all this duration of time, there are people who have been borrowing.”
“There are some who tried investing in certain things and it was not working out. But since they had been promised something big, they were having that hope. So, looking at this one-month salary, I feel it’s not going to go well for citizens here.”
“Though some of them might accept, generally, it’s not something good. at least if it was something that is more than three months, it would make some big deal. But just one month’s salary, that is something so bad.”

a4575.t:
Comme des hérons blancs autour d’un bovidé, les Européens s’accrochent aux Américains dans la gestion du conflit russo-ukrainien. Sans avoir une réelle influence dans les négociations qui se passent plutôt entre les présidents Trump et Poutine, certains Chefs d’Etat européens font des pieds et des mains, pour ne pas dire des courbettes pour être à la table.
En fin de compte, le Président Trump a fini par les convier. A quel prix ? Juste par courtoisie. On les a vus, accueillis par la cheffe du protocole de la Maison Blanche à leur arrivée et conduits dans une salle par ‘‘une porte dérobée’’, où ils ont eu ‘‘un déjeuner de travail’’ entre eux en attendant que le président américain finisse de s’entretenir avec son hôte, son vrai hôte, le président Zelenski qu’il a accueilli lui-même à la porte officielle de la Maison Blanche.
Ces invités ‘‘à peine désirables’’ sont à Washington, non pas pour avoir une quelconque influence sur le processus engagé par Trump, mais juste pour se faire bonne image aux yeux de leurs opinions publiques, lasses des répercussions d’une guerre qu’elles n’ont jamais soutenue.
On l’a vu au cours de cette rencontre de Washington. D’abord le premier moment d’échanges entre Trump et Zelenski a été retransmis en direct sur les médias américains. Le deuxième moment a été un huis clos dans le bureau ovale entre ces deux Chefs d’Etat. Enfin, c’est au troisième moment que le Président Trump est venu, par courtoisie, retrouver les autres chefs d’Etat qui se sont fait inviter pour écouter ce que chacun d’eux pense ou espère du processus.
De tout ce que ces dirigeants européens attendaient, le président Trump n’a donné aucune garantie. Il n’a pas annoncé un cessez-le-feu immédiat ; il a réitéré que l’accord sera une affaire à trois (Poutine-Trump-Zelenski) ; qu’il y aura des concessions territoriales (ayant appartenu à l’Ukraine) ; il n’y aura pas de troupes américaines en Ukraine. Et Trump trouve toujours en Poutine un interlocuteur crédible pour arriver à une solution durable à cette crise. Malgré les vaines tentatives de quelques médias européens de donner une certaine crédibilité à la présence des dirigeants européens à la Maison Blanche, les observateurs avertis ont perçu, dans cet épisode, la soumission presque servile des européens aux USA. Seul réconfort, ces dirigeants ont eu droit à une visite guidée de l’armoire où le président Trump range sa collection de casquettes MAGA ‘’Make America Great Again’’.
En définitive, c’est Trump et Poutine qui détiennent la clé pour mettre fin à ce conflit. Toute autre gesticulation n’est que pure prétention doublée d’une hallucination. Les Européens le savent. Et les prochains jours nous le confirmeront.
Siradji Sanda (ONEP)
a4575.en:
Op-ed: Barely desirable guests

Like white herons around a bovine, the Europeans cling to the Americans in the management of the Russo-Ukrainian conflict. Without having any real influence in the negotiations, which are taking place rather between Presidents Trump and Putin, certain European heads of state are bending over backwards - not to say bowing and scraping - to have a seat at the table.
In the end, President Trump ended up inviting them. At what price? Merely out of courtesy. We saw them, greeted by the White House chief of protocol on their arrival and led into a room through "a back door," where they had "a working lunch" among themselves while they waited for the American president to finish his talks with his guest, his real guest, President Zelensky, whom he welcomed himself at the official door of the White House.
These "barely desirable" guests are in Washington not to have any influence whatsoever on the process initiated by Trump, but merely to make themselves look good in the eyes of their publics, who are weary of the repercussions of a war they never supported.
This was plain to see during this Washington meeting. First, the opening moment of exchanges between Trump and Zelensky was broadcast live on the American media. The second moment was a closed-door session in the Oval Office between these two heads of state. Finally, it was at the third moment that President Trump came, out of courtesy, to join the other heads of state who had got themselves invited, to hear what each of them thinks or hopes for from the process.
Of everything these European leaders were expecting, President Trump gave no guarantee. He did not announce an immediate ceasefire; he reiterated that the agreement would be a three-way affair (Putin-Trump-Zelensky); that there would be territorial concessions (of land that had belonged to Ukraine); that there would be no American troops in Ukraine. And Trump still finds in Putin a credible interlocutor for arriving at a lasting solution to this crisis. Despite the vain attempts of some European media to lend a certain credibility to the presence of the European leaders at the White House, informed observers perceived, in this episode, the almost servile submission of the Europeans to the USA. Their only consolation: these leaders were given a guided tour of the cupboard where President Trump keeps his collection of MAGA "Make America Great Again" caps.
Ultimately, it is Trump and Putin who hold the key to ending this conflict. Any other posturing is pure pretension compounded by hallucination. The Europeans know it. And the coming days will confirm it for us.
Siradji Sanda (ONEP)

Commentaries | Jan 17,2026
The federal government will likely toss fuel subsidies entirely by the middle of next year. The Council of Ministers has passed a regulation that would see subsidies progressively lifted off in a year, with motorists carrying the full weight of global prices by July next year.
The regulation has introduced a six-month transition; the new scheme begins to apply on prices of benzene, diesel and kerosene products in July. An estimated 300,000 vehicles providing public transport services, excluding ride-hailing, will see a 10pc bi-annual rise in prices for five years. The remaining one million vehicle owners will be subjected to quarterly increases of 25pc for one year. Federal authorities believe the gradual lifting of fuel subsidies is necessary to ease the "burden endured by low-income segments of the population."
However, it is a move likely influenced by the growing federal budget deficit and ways of bridging it outside of monetary measures.
The federal government heavily subsidises fuel to the tune of around 25 billion Br last year through the Ethiopian Petroleum Supply Enterprise (EPSE). The Enterprise buys a litre of benzene at 44 Br, not including transportation costs. Despite the fluctuation of prices in the global market, domestic retail prices have only seen increases over the past years, unable to meet costs. Benzene is sold for 31.74 Br a litre at pumping stations and diesel for 28.94 Br.
Last month, the Ministry of Trade & Regional Integration adjusted fuel prices by record-high increments under the pressure of rising import bills. Its officials saw fit to cut subsidies by a quarter, leaving the cost to be shouldered by the public. The bill to import fuel - more than two billion dollars a year - is also rising. Fuel imports represented 11pc of the import bill last year. Though it was less than the preceding year in dollar terms, depreciation meant the figure was much higher in Birr.
Depreciation and rising costs in international markets have strained government coffers. The increasing prices have also tested the financial standing of the Enterprise, said Ahmed Tusa, acting head of the Petroleum & Energy Authority, during a media briefing last month. The lifting of the remaining 75pc in subsidies would push retail prices to over 50 Br a litre, not accounting for changes in the global market.
A barrel of Brent crude oil has seen prices more than double over the past year, hovering around 88 dollars last week. It was closer to 60 dollars three months ago.
Federal and regional authorities mandated to oversee the distribution will have to prepare to enforce the phasing out subsidy. The Ministry of Transport & Logistics is mandated to compile data on vehicles to continue receiving subsidies, including daily and monthly fuel consumption. It will enforce the installation and use of GPS technology on public transport vehicles and ensure that all cars have unique tags.
The Ministry of Finance will approve a receipt that the Petroleum Supply Enterprise will distribute to the 42 oil companies and the 1,200 gas stations operating under them.
The deficit incurred by oil companies and fuel retailers due to the gradual lifting of subsidies will be refunded by the Enterprise with interest, an official following the case disclosed. The refund period is not determined in the regulation, but it will be prompt not to hold up the companies' and dealers' working capital, according to this official. Dealers will be required to devise administrative procedures to distinguish vehicles that will continue buying fuel at subsidised prices.
Unless reimbursement is carried out on time, it will tie up cash for dealers who are already struggling to make cash-based payments for the fuel they receive, according to Ephrem Tesfaye, board member of the Petroleum Dealers' Association.
The illicit trade that could arise due to the dual-rate system is another concern raised by industry players. The regulation pledges stringent monitoring to prevent those receiving subsidised prices from selling fuel illegitimately. Administrative measures against those found in violation include revocation of subsidy privileges and criminal proceedings.
"I don't think the difference between the two prices is that attractive," said Ephrem.
He believes there is little to worry about illicit trade.
Officials of the Transport Ministry and the Authority have held discussions with managers of oil companies and dealers, giving them a detailed rundown of the scheme to be introduced next July.
"We'll see how efficient it will be," said Ephrem.
Teshager Amare, an economist and a consultant in commodity exchanges in African countries, argues in favour of keeping the subsidies. He worries any increase in the price of fuel comes with inflationary pressure. Headline inflation stood at 34pc in November.
Teshager sees the decision to lift subsidies as ill-timed. He advises officials to focus on developing a post-war recovery plan and rekindle economic activities before further removing subsidies lifts.
"Time should be taken to assess the impact of subsidies that have been lifted already," he said.
